On temporary marriage, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi take the verse to forbid it, whereas al-Zamakhshari argues that a temporary wife counts among the spouses if the marriage is valid. Al-Razi also reports Abu Hanifa's view that an exception does not affirm the opposite of what precedes it.

This verse states that whoever seeks gratification beyond his wife and what his right hand possesses is among those who transgress, the 'adūn. Most commentators agree on this plain meaning: al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, explains that these are people who pass from the lawful to the unlawful, and that the fornicator is counted among them. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi take it as forbidding fornication, sodomy and bestiality. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the neuter form ma malakat refers to female slaves and explain the grammar of the exception.

The ruling on temporary marriage (mut'a) is debated. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Kathir read the verse as prohibiting it, since the temporary partner is neither a wife nor a slave, and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad relies on the same reasoning. Al-Alusi reports differing positions, including one attributed to Ibn Abbas, which he regards as uncertain, and he gives the prohibition at length on the basis of hadiths.

On masturbation, most of the commentators cited, including al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, consider it forbidden under this verse, while Ahmad ibn Hanbal allowed it in cases of need, comparing it to bloodletting. Ibn Kathir also cites a report about a woman who took her slave, transmitted by Qatada and judged weak, and Ibn 'Ashur stresses the general sense of 'beyond that'.

In this verse God describes one of the qualities of the successful believers: they guard their trusts and their covenants and fulfil them faithfully. The commentators explain that a trust (amana) is anything entrusted to a person, and a covenant (ahd) is what one binds oneself to, whether toward God or toward people. Most read the verse as general, covering both the rights of God and the rights of people, including religious duties, deposits, oaths, contracts and vows, as al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti report. Ibn Kathir notes that keeping one's word and not betraying a trust are marks of the believer, in contrast with the signs of the hypocrite. Al-Razi holds that the trust is broader than the covenant, since every covenant is a trust, while Ibn Ashur observes that trusts usually concern precious items that one fears may be lost. The majority reads the word in the plural, while Ibn Kathir reads it in the singular; al-Zamakhshari explains that the word, as a verbal noun, allows both forms. Al-Baydawi notes that the verse links trusts with prayer and that commentators differ on whether the covenant concerns the bond between the servant and his Lord or between people. Al-Jaza'iri includes the ritual bath among the trusts. Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith in which breaking a trust is one of three signs of the hypocrite.

This verse describes one of the qualities of the believers who attain success: they guard their prayers, meaning they take care to perform them and to persist in them. The commentators broadly agree on the general sense. Al-Tabari reports that Masruq, Ibrahim and others understood it as performing the prayer at its proper time, and Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Mas'ud defining guarding as keeping to the times, adding that abandoning prayer is disbelief. Abu al-Duha, 'Alqama, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrima also stress the times, while Qatada adds the bowing and prostration. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di link this guarding to constancy and to completing its pillars. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i takes constancy to refer to the obligatory prayers. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain why prayer is mentioned again: humility in prayer is distinct from guarding it, the first concerning the quality of the act and the second its faithful observance. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi debate whether humility is one of the obligations of prayer or only one of its virtues; al-Razi holds that it is obligatory, though the question is not settled for everyone. As for the end of the verse, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect inheriting to dwellings: each person has a place in paradise and a place in hell, and believers inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers. On the word firdaws, al-Hasan takes it as a name of paradise, Abu Hurayra as a mountain of paradise, Mujahid as a Roman word arabized, and al-Dahhak as an Arabic word meaning vineyard.

This verse identifies as the true inheritors those who possess the qualities listed earlier in the sura, such as humility in prayer, guarding trusts and pledges, and being constant in the prayers. The commentators say they deserve to be called inheritors, and what they inherit is the Firdaws, where they will dwell forever.

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, explain the inheritance by saying that every person has a dwelling in Paradise and one in Hell; if a believer enters Paradise, the people of Hell inherit his place there, while a disbeliever loses his place in Paradise, as reported in a hadith from Abu Hurayra. Ibn Kathir and others link this meaning to a report from Mujahid. Al-Razi understands the inheritance as Paradise passing to the believers without prior reckoning, much like property passing to an heir. Ibn Ashur sees it as a metaphor for a secured entitlement.

The commentators agree that the Firdaws is the highest or central part of Paradise, and that the word sometimes refers to Paradise as a whole. They differ on its origin: Mujahid and al-Zajjaj consider it a Greek or Roman word arabized, others say Persian or Ethiopian, while al-Dahhak takes it to be Arabic, meaning a vineyard. Abu Hurayra describes it as the mountain of Paradise from which its rivers flow.

Some commentators hold that these qualities mean that their possessors remain in the Firdaws forever, without ever leaving or dying. Al-Qurtubi also cites a tradition that whoever observes these ten verses enters Paradise, which Ibn al-Arabi considered sound, though others regarded it as weak.

This verse states that those who succeed are the ones who inherit the Firdaws, meaning the highest and most excellent part of Paradise, and that they will remain in it forever, never leaving it or dying. The commentators explain that the word inherit is a metaphor for deserving this abode through one's deeds. They agree that the Firdaws refers to Paradise as a whole or to its highest part.

On the origin of the word, opinions differ. Mujahid and al-Zajjaj hold that it is a Roman word that was Arabized, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima relate it to Ethiopian or Persian, while al-Dahhak takes it to be an Arabic word meaning a vineyard or a garden thick with trees. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir report that some early scholars said a garden is only called firdaws if it contains grapevines.

As for the inheritance, most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, cite the hadith that every person has a dwelling in Paradise and one in Hell, and that whoever enters Paradise inherits the dwelling of the one destined for Hell. Mujahid adds that the believer's house in Hell is demolished and his house in Paradise is built. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi describe the Firdaws as a vast garden containing all kinds of fruit. Several hadiths about God planting the garden with His own hand are considered weak or strange by a number of scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir.

The commentators agree that the verse addresses the believers described by the preceding qualities, especially humility in prayer and guarding the prayers, and that khulud means lasting permanence without end.

This verse says that God created man from an extract drawn out of clay. The commentators differ on who is meant by "man": al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others understand Adam, who was drawn from clay, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and many others understand the human race, with "sulala" meaning the drop of semen drawn from the loins, or the purest essence of water, and "clay" meaning Adam from whom mankind descends. Al-Tabari preferred this second view because of the following words "then We made him a drop in a firm lodging"; Ibn Kathir found the first view clearer and closer to the context. On the meaning of the word there is broad agreement: the sulala is what is drawn out of something, its essence, and semen and offspring are both called sulala or sulail. Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi observe that the pattern fu'ala signifies smallness. Al-Kalbi reports that it is the clay which, when squeezed, lets liquid slip out between the fingers, and Aban b. Taghlib says it is dust. The commentators cite the report of 'Umar, who said "blessed is God, the best of creators" when the verse was revealed. Razi explains that khalq here means measuring and shaping, and that creation in the sense of bringing into being belongs to God alone. Most agree on the successive stages of drop, clinging clot, lump of flesh, and then the "other creation", which most take to be the breathing of the spirit into the foetus, while others mention birth into the world, the growth of hair or the full flowering of youth.

This verse describes one stage in the creation of the human being. The commentators explain that "placing" means setting the drop of semen in the womb, a firm and well-protected place. They differ on who "the human" refers to: Qatada holds it is Adam, created from clay, while Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima take it to mean Adam's descendants, the "extract" then being the essence of water. All agree on the successive stages: the drop, the clinging clot, the lump of flesh, then bones clothed in flesh. As for the "other creation" that follows, the views vary. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliya, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd understand it as the breathing of the spirit into the body, which al-Tabari chooses as the most sound view. Ibn Abbas also gives the sense of coming forth into the world, Qatada the growth of hair and teeth, and Mujahid the full flowering of youth. Ibn Atiyya considers these restrictions unfounded and holds that the verse covers all these stages together. On the phrase "the best of creators", Mujahid takes it to mean the best of makers, and several scholars note that the word khalq can mean shaping or measuring, as in a line of Zuhayr, while others stress that true creation from nothing belongs to God alone. Reports about the occasion of the revelation of this phrase are cited, though Ibn Kathir considers some of them weak.

This verse describes the stages of human creation in the womb: a person is first made from an extract of clay, then becomes a drop of semen placed in a secure womb, then a clot of blood, then a piece of flesh the size of a mouthful, then bones form and are covered with flesh. Then God produces another creation. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand this as the breathing of the spirit into the foetus, a view also reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and others. Al-Baghawi notes this view and another attributed to Ibn Abbas, that it refers to the stages of life after birth, from childhood to old age, to the growth of hair and teeth, or to reaching maturity according to Mujahid, while al-Hasan says it refers to being male or female. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi list these opinions at length. On the phrase "blessed is God, the best of creators", al-Tabari reports Mujahid's view that khaliq means maker, supported by a line of Zuhayr, and Ibn Jurayj's view that Jesus also created; al-Tabari prefers Mujahid's view. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain the grammar of the superlative, and several works report that Umar spoke these words before the Prophet confirmed them, a report Ibn Kathir considers weak. The verse concludes that people will die after this and be raised on the Day of Resurrection.

This verse states that after the successive stages of human creation, from clay to a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, bones clothed in flesh and finally the breathing of the soul, every human being is destined to die. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the word "mayyitun" refers to someone who will die in the future, whereas "mayyit" describes one who has already died. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw the same distinction, noting that "mayyit" expresses a lasting state while "ma'it" refers to an event yet to happen. Al-Qurtubi reports that al-Farra' and others state that the Arabs do not use "ma'it" for one who has died.

The meaning of "sulala", an extracted essence, is discussed. Qatada and, in one transmission, Ibn Abbas take it to mean Adam, who was drawn from clay. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others understand it as the drop of semen extracted from the father. Al-Kalbi describes it as the clay that trickles out between the fingers when pressed.

Al-Razi argues that the mention of death here serves to show that the Creator does not leave His creation without an end, and that death comes before the resurrection announced in the next verse. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse uses "then" to indicate a gap between creation and death, and that the emphasis on death is meant to warn the listener not to forget the end of life.

The phrase "another creation" has been read in several ways. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak, take it to mean the breathing of the soul into the body, which al-Tabari prefers. Qatada understands it as the growth of teeth and hair, Mujahid as the full maturity of youth, and al-Hasan as the distinction between male and female. Al-Ghawfi, relying on Ibn Abbas, describes it as the stages of life after birth. Ibn Kathir notes that these views are not contradictory, since they describe successive phases.

This verse states that after the successive stages of human creation, from drop of semen to clot to lump of flesh, and after the breathing of the spirit, people will die and then be raised on the Day of Resurrection for reckoning and recompense. Commentators explain that the phrase "then indeed you will die" describes a state that will befall them and did not exist before: the Arabs say of one not yet dead "ma'it" or "mayyit soon," but not "ma'it" of one who has already died, as al-Tabari, al-Farra', Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari report. Some readers recited "la-ma'itun" with an alif, and al-Zamakhshari distinguishes mayyit as a settled quality from ma'it as something that is occurring. For al-Razi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir, the resurrection meant is the general resurrection on the Last Day, not merely life in the grave; mentioning creation, death and resurrection points to three kinds of divine power without denying life in the grave. The meaning of "another creation" varies: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak and Abu al-'Aliya take it as the breathing of the spirit, which al-Tabari prefers, while Qatada takes it as the growth of teeth and hair, Mujahid as reaching full youth, al-Hasan as being male or female, and al-'Awfi, citing Ibn 'Abbas, as the sequence of states from birth to old age. Overall, the verse establishes that human life runs from creation through death to resurrection, when each person will be judged and repaid.

God says in this verse that He created seven heavens above the people, one above another. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, explain that they are called tara'iq because they are layered like the soles of sandals laid one on the other, and they identify the verse's subject as the seven heavens. Others, such as al-Mawardi, Ibn Qutayba and al-Baydawi, add that they are the paths of the angels or the courses of the stars, and al-Baghawi notes that each heaven has its own form. As for the phrase 'and We were not unaware of the creation', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read it as God's protection of the sky from falling on people, citing the verse in Surat al-Hajj that He holds up the heavens. Al-Hasan understands it as God's sending of rain down to them, while Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy widen it to God's care for all creatures and their needs. The commentators agree that the passage recounts God's favours: water sent down in measure, gardens of palms and vines, the olive tree of Mount Sinai that yields oil and relish for eaters, and the livestock that provide milk, food, and transport by land and sea. Ibn 'Ashur sees this as a reminder that the heavenly realms were made with wisdom, and al-Shawkani links the passage to the resurrection announced just before.

This verse says that God sends down water from the sky in a measured amount, sufficient for people, crops and animals, and settles it in the earth where it can be drawn from wells, springs and pools. It then warns that He is able to take it away, a reminder that calls for gratitude. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, understand the water as rain, and many add that all water on earth comes from the sky. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi stress that the measure is precise, neither so great as to destroy nor so small as to fail. Mujahid, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that all earthly water originates from the sky, Ibn Atiyya suggesting this refers to sweet water, since salt water remains in drought. Another view, reported by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, is that the verse means the four or five rivers sent down from Paradise, a report that Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi regard as weakly transmitted and not accepted as the verse's meaning. The phrase bi-qadar is generally read as a measure fitted to need, and al-Alusi and al-Zamakhshari note that the indefinite word for withdrawal makes the threat stronger than the one in Surat al-Mulk. Several scholars, including al-Tabari, explain that the palm and the vine are named for their prominence in the Hijaz, and the verse's mention of the olive, which yields oil for anointing and seasoning, is generally read as a continuation of this blessing.

The commentators explain that God reminds His servants of His favours: He sends down water from the sky in a measured amount, lodges it in the earth, and by it brings forth for people gardens of palm trees and vines, containing many fruits on which they feast and by which they are nourished. These two kinds are named because they were the best known to the Arabs and among the most useful: palms were chiefly grown in Medina and vines in Ta'if. All agree that the word 'gardens' means orchards, and that 'fruits' covers everything beyond palms and vines. Scholars differ over what the pronouns 'in them' and 'from them' refer to: al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take them to mean the gardens in general, while others take them to refer only to the palm and the vine, which yield many varieties of fresh dates, grapes, dried dates, raisins and syrups. Jurists such as al-Qurtubi draw on the verse in the question of one who swears not to eat fruit: Abu Hanifa excludes fresh dates, grapes and pomegranates, while his two companions include them. As for the tree mentioned next, most commentators identify it as the olive tree that grows from Mount Sinai, between Egypt and Aqaba, whose oil is used for anointing and as a relish for bread. The scholars differ on the meaning of the name Sinai: blessing, beauty, or abundance of trees.

This verse speaks of the olive tree that grows from Mount Sinai, listed among the blessings that follow the mention of the heavens, the water and the gardens. The commentators agree that the tree is the olive, whose fruit yields oil used for anointing and for lamps, and in which bread is dipped as a condiment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the olive is singled out for the great benefits it gives and because little care is taken to water it, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it more broadly as any tree yielding oil, according to the region. The word Sayna' has been read in several ways: Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas in one report took it to mean blessed, Qatada and al-Dahhak took it to mean beautiful in Nabataean, while Muqatil, Ibn Zayd and most exegetes regard it as the name of the mountain or the region where Moses was addressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi favour this last view. On the reading tunbitu, al-Tabari considers the two forms to have the same meaning, Abu 'Ubayda holds that the particle bi is superfluous, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi supposes an implied object. Ibn Kathir cites hadiths praising olive oil for eating and anointing, some of which are judged weak. The overall meaning remains a divine blessing from which oil and food are obtained.

The commentators explain that God directs attention to the cattle, namely camels, cows and sheep, as a sign through which people can reflect and recognise His power and favours. The sign lies in the pure, pleasant milk that comes out from between the contents of the stomach and the blood, in the many benefits drawn from them such as wool, hair, hides and offspring, and in the meat people eat. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir give closely similar explanations. Ibn Kathir reports that the Arabs carried their loads on camels, while al-Qurtubi holds that the words 'and upon them' refer to camels on land, with ships at sea. The readings of 'we give you to drink' differ: Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, through Abu Bakr, read with a fatha, while the others read with a damma. Some philologists treat saqa and asqa as synonyms, whereas others, such as al-Farra', distinguish them: the first for giving a drink directly, the second for providing a drink that is kept in store. Al-Razi stresses that the milk is pure, pleasant and separated from what is impure. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that the camel is singled out for riding and carrying because it is the animal most commonly used for this. On the general meaning the commentators agree: the verse enumerates God's favours and calls for gratitude.

The commentators explain that the verse recalls God's favour: people are carried on livestock on land and on ships at sea. Most take the pronoun "upon them" to refer to the cattle in general, so that transport is done on some of them, such as camels. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud, however, hold that "the cattle" here means camels alone, since these are the animals normally ridden and loaded, and they fit the pairing with ships, which are called the ships of the land; they cite Dhu al-Rumma's line about a land vessel whose reins lie beneath his cheek. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain the metaphor in that line. Al-Alusi finds it acceptable that camels are understood by implication, though not as the primary sense. Al-Qurtubi notes that carrying on land is done only on camels, so the pronoun may refer to some of the cattle, and he leaves the choice open. All agree the verse is a sign of blessing and a proof of divine power and wisdom, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di draw out the call to gratitude. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a transition preparing the story of Noah.

This verse reports that God sent Noah to his people, and that he called them to worship God alone, since there is no deity worthy of worship besides Him, and to fear His punishment. The commentators see in it the opening of Noah's story, which consoles the Prophet ﷺ and warns the Quraysh. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that 'worship God' means devote worship to Him alone, and that 'will you not fear Him' means will you not fear His punishment if you worship other than Him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that 'You have no god other than Him' gives the reason for the command to worship. The word 'ghayruhu' may be read in the nominative or the genitive, depending on how one analyses its place in the sentence. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan detail the objections of the chiefs: a mere human cannot be a messenger, God would have sent angels, their forefathers never heard of this, and Noah is mad. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi identify the chiefs (al-mala') as the notables and leaders. Al-Tabari says that 'jinna' means madness, while al-Zamakhshari notes it may also refer to jinn. On 'wait for him for a time', opinions differ: waiting for his death, according to Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, or waiting until his madness becomes evident, according to al-Mawardi. Al-Tabari notes that the time is not specific. The passage ends with Noah's prayer asking God to help him against their denial.

This verse reports what the chiefs of Noah's people, who disbelieved, said to their followers when they rejected his call to worship God alone. They claimed he was merely a human like them, distinguished by nothing, and that his real aim was to gain superiority and lead them. They added that if God had wished to send a messenger, He would have sent angels, and that they had never heard of such a thing from their forefathers. They also accused him of madness and told their people to wait until his fate became clear or he died. The commentators generally read these words as a refusal to accept that a human being could receive a divine mission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya largely agree on this basic sense. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari explain "yatafaddal" as seeking superiority and leadership, and al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy read it similarly as a desire to rule. On "hatta hin", al-Tabari takes it as an unspecified period, while al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand it as waiting for his death or for his madness to become evident. Al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider the charge of madness baseless, since his opponents knew his sound mind. Ibn Kathir sees in the phrase "what we have not heard of among our forefathers" a sign of a long gap since earlier prophets, while others read it as stubborn denial. Ibn 'Ashur notes that Noah was the first messenger sent to all the earth. The passage ends with Noah's prayer asking God for help against those who denied him.

The commentators explain that the chiefs of Noah's people, who rejected his message, said that Noah was merely a man like themselves who wanted to rise above them, that had God wished to send a messenger He would have sent angels, and that they had never heard of such a thing among their forefathers. They then declared that he was a man possessed by madness, and told the people to wait for him for a while. Most read this as waiting until he recovers his sanity or dies so that they may be rid of him, while al-Farra' notes that the word hin refers to an unspecified period of time. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Noah then asked his Lord to help him against their denial.

The commentators agree that the verse quotes the disbelievers' words and that jinna means madness. They differ on whether the word can also mean jinn, which is the reading of Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, who explain that the madness was thought to come from an afflicting jinn. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan add that the notables meant to endure him until his situation became clear, and that they would kill him if he did not recover. Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud point out the inconsistency of their charges, since they accused him both of seeking leadership and of being insane.

Al-Razi, al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di examine the objections one by one and find them weak: being human does not disqualify a prophet, the absence of precedent does not prove that something is impossible, and Noah's speech itself shows sound reason. Ibn 'Ashur calls the argument from not having heard of it a sophistical reasoning. Al-Sha'rawi and al-Jaza'iri draw a parallel with the accusations made against the Prophet Muhammad. The verse also has several recitation variants for the words rabb and kadhdhabuni, which Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi record without drawing any legal conclusion from them.

This verse reports that Noah, after his people rejected him and persisted in disbelief until he despaired of their faith, asked his Lord to help him against them because of their denial. The commentators generally agree that this help means their destruction and retribution against them, and that the particle bima expresses cause: that God would destroy them as punishment for their denial. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi, however, read it as substitution: help me in place of their denial, that is, let the joy of victory over them replace the grief of their rejection, or carry out the threatened punishment they denied. Ibn Kathir, al-Sam'ani and Abu Hayyan keep to the sense of a plea for their destruction. Ibn 'Ashur explains that Noah, knowing that only those who had already believed would be saved, asked for a specific help: the annihilation of the unbelievers, as mentioned in Surah Nuh. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand the denial as their rejection of what he conveyed from his Lord. The following verses explain that God ordered him to build the ark under His eyes and by His revelation, to take aboard a pair of every kind and his family except those against whom the word had already gone forth, and not to plead for the wrongdoers, for they would be drowned. Regarding the tannur that boiled over, the majority, including al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Razi, take it to be the ordinary bread oven.

The commentators explain that God answered Noah's plea for help against a people who had denied him. He revealed to him that he should build the ark under His watch and protection, and that He would teach him how to build it. The sign of the coming punishment would be the bubbling of the oven. Noah was then to take aboard a pair of every kind, male and female, along with his household, except for the one against whom the word had already been decreed. He was forbidden to plead on behalf of those who had done wrong, for they were certain to drown. The commentators agree that the command refers to the punishment and that the revelation is teaching and guidance. About the word tannur, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take it to be the ordinary bread oven, and some report it was Adam's oven passed to Noah, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi record differing views on its location, such as Kufa, Syria or India. Ibn Abbas understood it as the surface of the earth, Qatada as its highest point, and Ali as the break of dawn, while al-Mawardi and others read it as an expression for the severity of the matter. Readers differ on whether kullin is read with tanwin or as a construct. As for the household, most take it to mean his wife and children, whereas Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi take it to mean those who believed with him, excluding his disbelieving son and wife. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that it refers to kinship of faith.

The commentators explain that God told Noah, once he and those with him were settled on the ark, to praise God for delivering them from the wrongdoing people, meaning the unbelievers and idolaters. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the plain sense: Noah rose up and settled in the ship, and praising God for the rescue includes praising Him for the destruction of the people. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the command is addressed to Noah alone because he was their prophet and leader, so his words count as theirs, which also honours the rank of prophethood.

There are some differences of detail. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the verb to mean sitting or riding upright on board, while al-Sam'ani and al-Sha'rawi also understand it as rising high. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the prohibition on pleading for the unbelievers comes alongside the command to praise God for their ruin, which underlines that their destruction had already been decreed. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the rescue meant being removed from their company and conduct, which harmed the believers.

The commentators agree on the general lesson of gratitude for the believers on board. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri draw from the verse the practice of praising God on boarding a ship, and of asking for a blessed landing afterwards. Al-Qasimi and al-Alusi observe that thankfulness for the rescue also includes thanks for the removal of the harm.

After Noah and those with him had settled into the ark and praised God for their deliverance, God instructs him to pray: "My Lord, cause me to disembark at a blessed landing, for You are the best of those who bring down." Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand this as Noah's descent from the ark to dry land, with the blessing being the multiplication of his offspring through his three sons; Mujahid adds that the prayer was said as he came out of the ark. Another view, held by al-Razi and by Ibn 'Atiyya in one formulation, takes the place to be the ark itself, so that the prayer asks for safety while he remains aboard. Readers differ on the vocalisation of the word: most read "munzalan" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the zay, as a verbal noun meaning the act of bringing down, while Abu Bakr, through Asim, reads "manzilan" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay, meaning the place of landing; some scholars distinguish the two meanings. Al-Qurtubi sees the verse as a lesson for believers, who should recite this supplication when mounting and dismounting a vessel or mount, and he reports that Ali used to say it on entering the mosque. The closing phrase, "Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were ever testing," is explained by al-Tabari as a test of the peoples, a trial that leads to punishment or to a warning, and al-Razi argues that the test may also concern future generations of those who are responsible.

This verse closes the account of Noah by stating that in what God did to Noah's people, in the ark and in the destruction of the disbelievers, there are signs and lessons, and that God tests His servants by sending messengers and warning them before the punishment falls. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the signs are proofs of God's power and of the prophets' truthfulness, and that the verse addresses the Quraysh so they may take heed of what befell earlier nations. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy see the destruction of the deniers and the rescue of the believers as among the greatest lessons. The meaning of the trial is where opinions differ. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand it as a test through warning and admonition, so that it becomes clear who will take heed. Al-Qurtubi clarifies that this does not mean God gains new knowledge, but that the people's condition is made manifest to the angels. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a divine law that separates the good from the bad, and al-Sha'rawi notes that trials also befall believers to purify their faith and raise their rank. Al-Jaza'iri stresses that the test applies to both believer and unbeliever so that divine justice appears. On the particle inna, the commentators take it as the lightened form of the heavy particle with the distinguishing lam, and al-Tabari reads kunna as meaning 'and we had been'.

God says that after the people of Noah were destroyed, He brought into being another generation, another people. The commentators differ on who they were. Ibn Abbas and most exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Alusi, hold that they were the people of 'Ad, pointing out that their story follows that of Noah in al-A'raf, Hud and al-Shu'ara, and Hud's words in al-A'raf: remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and, in another passage, Ibn Kathir identify them as Thamud, destroyed by the Cry, whose prophet was Salih, citing the mention of the Cry at the end of the story. On both views the messenger was one of their own people, who called them to worship God alone and to fear Him. The commentaries agree that the notables rejected him, saying he was only a human who eats and drinks as they do, and denied resurrection, saying far, far is what you are promised. They were then seized by the Cry, and became like the foam the torrent carries away. Opinions differ on their identity, but there is broad agreement on the call itself and on the fate of those who disbelieved.

This verse tells us that after the destruction of Noah's people, God raised up another generation and sent among them a messenger of their own kind, who called them to worship God alone, told them they had no deity other than Him, and urged them to guard against His punishment. The commentators differ on who this generation was. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify them as the people of 'Ad and their prophet Hud, pointing to the story of Hud that follows Noah's in al-A'raf, Hud and al-Shu'ara, and to Hud's words reminding his people that God made them successors after Noah's people. Al-Tabari, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and Ibn 'Ashur favour Thamud and their prophet Salih, relying on the mention of the mighty blast at the end of the account, which struck Thamud rather than 'Ad. On the phrase 'an u'budu Allah', most read it as an explanation of the sending: We told them through the messenger to worship God. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the community or town was treated as the place of the sending. The commentators agree that this call to monotheism is the first call every prophet makes to his people. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the messenger came from their own lineage so that they would be more inclined to listen, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that this stress on his being one of them serves to match their situation with that of the people addressed by Muhammad.

This verse reports what the chiefs of the people who disbelieved and denied the meeting in the Hereafter said. Their worldly comfort had made them proud. They claimed that the messenger is only a human like them, who eats what they eat and drinks what they drink, so he has no superiority over them.

The commentators agree on the central meaning: the notables rejected the prophet by pointing to his human nature. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di explain that they found it strange that a messenger should come from among men rather than an angel, and that their refusal grew from arrogance and from denial of bodily resurrection. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy see three roots in the verse: disbelief in the Creator, denial of the Hereafter, and absorption in worldly pleasure. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the word for affluence means lavish comfort, and Sayyid Qutb adds that prosperity tends to harden hearts.

On the identity of the people, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di hold that they are Thamud and their prophet Salih, while al-Razi reports that Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes name Hud and the people of 'Ad. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the reports point toward 'Ad.

On the wording, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain the use of the conjunction by saying that their speech was not directly connected to the prophet's words, while al-Zamakhshari sees it as joining truth and falsehood within the same event. Al-Qurtubi reports that al-Farra' takes the word min as omitted in mimma tashrabun, a view the Basran grammarians reject. The verse also shows how they regarded obedience to a fellow human as a loss, as al-Qasimi observes.

The verse reports the words of the eminent men of Hud's people, who denied the meeting with the Hereafter and had been made proud by ease and comfort. They tell their people that this messenger is only a human being who eats and drinks as they do, so he has no special status over them, and that obeying him would make them losers. They also deny resurrection after they have become dust and bones. The commentators agree on the core meaning: for these leaders, following a man like themselves is a loss of dignity and sound judgment. Al-Tabari explains that the particle lam introduces an oath and that idhan links the condition to its result, and he notes that the repeated annakum is due to the length of the sentence, as in a reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Farra, al-Jurmi and al-Mubarrad take the repetition as emphasis, while al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj offer other analyses. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand the loss as a loss of reason and opinion, whereas al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud see loss both in this world and the next. Al-Razi notes that the notables count obedience to the messenger as a loss but not worship of idols. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri draw from it a warning against rejecting the messenger. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that the messenger is not merely a man like them, since he receives revelation.

This verse relates the words of the chiefs of the people of Salih, or, in other readings, of the people of Hud, who deny resurrection after death. For most exegetes the meaning is: does this messenger promise you that, once you have died and become dust and bones without flesh, you will be brought out alive from your graves as you were before? They use the question form to express disbelief and mockery.

The commentators agree that the second "annakum" repeats the first, for emphasis after a long interruption, and that "mukhrajun" is the predicate. This is the view of al-Farra, al-Jarmi, al-Mubarrad, and of al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi. Sibawayh treats the second as an appositive to the first, with the predicate of the first left implicit as "tub'athun", and it is this implicit verb that governs "idha". Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud offer another analysis in which "annakum mukhrajun" is the subject and "idha mittum" the predicate, meaning your bringing out will occur when you die. Ibn Mas'ud's reading omits the first "annakum".

As for "hayhat hayhat", it expresses remoteness; grammarians debate whether it is a verb or a noun, and its readings vary. Its repetition, according to most, stresses how implausible they found the claim. Al-Razi, al-Biqa'i and Ibn Ashur explain that the denial concerned bodily resurrection in complete human form on the Day of Judgment, and that their rejection rested on the states of death and decay.

The Qur'an records the people of Hud dismissing the promise of resurrection with the words "Far, far is what you are promised!", meaning that being raised alive from the graves after becoming dust and bones is utterly remote. The commentators agree that "hayhat" is a word meaning "far away" or "it is distant", repeated for emphasis and to express a sense of regret, and that the lam before "lima" specifies what is deemed remote. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the meaning is that such a resurrection is extremely unlikely. On the grammar, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat the subject as implied, referring to the resurrection or the coming out from the graves, while al-Zajjaj takes the word as a verbal noun; al-Zamakhshari compares the lam with that of "hayta laka". Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i differ on how to pause on the final sound, one with the hā' and the other with the tā'. The recitations vary in vowelling, with fatha, kasra, damma and tanwin, and the exegetes accept these as valid dialects. As for their statement "It is only our life in this world: we die and we live", al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read it as generations passing away and replacing one another, al-Mawardi gives three interpretations, including the reversal of the order of the verbs, and Ibn 'Atiyya presents it as the denial of the Dahriyya.

This verse reports the words of the chiefs of Hud's people, who denied the meeting with the Hereafter and rejected resurrection. They said, 'Far-fetched, far-fetched is what you are promised,' meaning that what they were told seemed extremely unlikely. They then added, 'There is only our life of this world: we die and we live,' meaning there is no other life, and that some people die while others are born. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the purpose of the statement is to deny resurrection, and that 'hayhat' expresses distance. Ibn Abbas explained the word as meaning distance, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya discuss its different readings and grammatical uses. On the meaning of 'we die and we live', the commentators differ. Ibn Isa, Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Kalbi take it to mean the death of one generation and the life of the next, or fathers dying while sons live. Others, including al-Sam'ani, al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i, understand the words to be inverted in order, meaning 'we live and then die.' Al-Zajjaj notes that the particle 'wa' does not imply sequence. Al-Alusi raises the possibility of a metempsychosis reading, without deciding. Ibn Ashur explains that the pronoun 'hiya' refers to the life implied by the speech, and some commentators see this statement as the disbelief of materialists.

This verse reports the words of the leaders of a people who dismissed their prophet as a mere man who fabricates lies against God, refusing to believe him. Al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan hold that the people were Thamud and the prophet Salih, while most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, say they were the people of Hud, ‘Ad. These leaders denied monotheism and resurrection, insisting that there is only this worldly life, in which one generation dies and another is born. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that they were given luxury and wealth, which made them proud. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di report that when the prophet despaired of their faith, he prayed to his Lord for victory, and God answered him by announcing their late regret, which would not help them. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi state that they were seized by the Cry in truth and became like the withered debris carried by a flood. On the meaning of ghuthaʾ, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say it is dried, decayed wood, while al-Mawardi cites foam or fallen leaves. Al-Razi considers the Cry to be the shout of Gabriel, though he also mentions a quake or the punishment itself. Commentators agree that the destruction was just, and that the curse of distance fell on them. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur discuss the word hayhat, meaning something like 'far, far away', with its several recitations.

This passage recounts the prayer of the prophet, Hud or Salih according to the commentators, when he despaired of his people's faith: 'My Lord, grant me victory because they have called me a liar.' God answers that his opponents will soon be filled with regret. Commentators agree that this was a supplication made after all means of preaching had been exhausted, and that the victory sought meant God's vengeance through their destruction. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the people perished by a cry accompanied by a violent wind. The disagreement concerns their identity. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, as al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note, identify them as 'Ad with the prophet Hud, whereas Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Tabari identify them as Thamud with Salih, and al-Baydawi relies on the cry to make the same identification. On the nature of the cry, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of an earthquake, Zamakhshari and Qurtubi of a cry from Gabriel, and al-Hasan of death itself. All agree that 'ghuthaa' means the debris and foam carried by a torrent, and that 'fa-bu'dan' is a curse of perdition. Sayyid Qutb stresses that the affluent reject faith out of arrogance, while al-Sha'rawi sees this prayer as that of one who has exhausted all means.

This verse records God's answer to His prophet, who had called down judgment on his people after they called him a liar: they will soon regret it. The commentators agree that the regret will come when they witness the punishment, and that it will then be of no benefit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take the people to be Thamud, the people of Salih, while al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say that most scholars identify them as the people of Hud, a view al-Razi describes as the most common. All of them see the 'shout' (al-sayha) as the punishment that seized them, and most attribute it to the cry of Gabriel; Ibn Abbas understands it as a violent quake, while al-Hasan takes it to be the punishment and death itself. The phrase 'bil-haqq' is explained as meaning that the destruction was just, since they deserved it, or that it came from God's justice. The word 'ghuthaa', the foam or debris carried by a flood, describes people reduced to nothing and of no use; al-Tabari reads this as a parable. 'Fa-bu'dan' is a curse of distance and ruin, or simply a statement according to al-Baydawi. On grammar, opinions differ: 'ma' in 'amma qalil' is either superfluous, emphasising how short the time is, or an indefinite noun qualified by 'qalil'; Ibn Ashur takes 'an' to mean 'after'.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the destruction of the people who denied their prophet, after he had called for their punishment. A mighty cry seized them in truth, meaning in justice and as they deserved for their disbelief, and they were reduced to a wreckage without benefit, like the foam and debris that a flood carries away. Most agree on the meaning of ghuthaa': dry, rotten vegetation or a worthless thing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be dead wood, Qutrub dry leaves that fell into water, and al-Akhfash the scum and refuse carried by the water. As for the cry, Ibn 'Abbas understood it as a violent quaking, many as the cry of Gabriel, and al-Hasan as death and punishment itself. On the identity of the people, most scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, hold that they were the people of Hud, the 'Ad, while al-Tabari and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi say they were Thamud and the prophet Salih, a view Ibn 'Ashur also favours. The phrase fa-bu'dan is understood either as a curse or as a statement of their ruin and their distance from mercy. Al-Zamakhshari treats the lam after it as clarifying who is meant by the curse, and al-Mawardi reports two readings: removal from mercy, or an increase in punishment.

This verse says that after the earlier peoples were destroyed, God brought forth other generations, the word qarn meaning here a people or a generation. The commentators differ on who they were. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Shawkani and Ibn Ashur identify them with the peoples of Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, among others. Ibn 'Abbas, reported by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, takes them to be the Children of Israel, while al-Razi reads the verse as a general summary of earlier stories and notes that God never left the lands without accountable people. Al-Tabari sees in what follows a warning to the polytheists of the Prophet's community: their respite lasts only until their appointed term, as it did for earlier nations. The commentators agree that every nation has a fixed term that it can neither hasten nor delay. Al-Razi considers whether this term is the length of life or the time of death and leans toward the latter. Al-Kacbi, as quoted by al-Razi, holds that God destroys a people only when He knows they will grow only more stubborn. On the word tatra, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand messengers coming one after another, some adding that there was an interval between them, whereas Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhshari describe an unbroken succession. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the reading with tanwin belongs to Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr. The word ahadith means things spoken of as examples or lessons, and al-Akhfash, cited by al-Qurtubi, notes that the phrase is used only for evil.

This verse states that every nation has a fixed term set by God, which it can neither advance nor delay. Most commentators understand that each people's destruction comes at the moment God has decreed. Al-Tabari reads it as a warning to the idolaters of the Prophet's community: God delays them so that they may reach their term, and then punishment will strike them as it struck earlier nations. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di explain that the nations follow one another, generation after generation, as written in the preserved Tablet. Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, identifies the 'other generations' with the Children of Israel, while most name the peoples of Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. Al-Razi reports al-Ka'bi's view that the term is the moment of punishment, which God fixes in relation to whether a people will believe, and that He destroys a people only when He knows they will not believe. Al-Razi also notes that the term may mean the span of life or the moment of death, the latter being the more obvious sense, and Ash'arite scholars draw from the verse that a person killed dies at his appointed term. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi state that no nation is destroyed before its term arrives, nor is its term postponed even an hour. Ibn Ashur sees the phrase as an explanatory aside answering the question of how long these peoples lasted. Al-Jaza'iri and al-Muyassar give the plain reading: no nation hastens or delays its appointed time.

This verse says that after the earlier nations, God sent His messengers one after another. Each time a nation received its messenger, it denied him, so God destroyed the peoples in succession until they became mere stories told and taken as lessons. The verse closes with a curse of distance from mercy upon a people who do not believe. The commentators agree that tatran means messengers following one another. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as an unbroken succession, while al-Mawardi reports two possible meanings: messengers coming one after another, or messengers separated by long intervals. On the root, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi link the word to witr, meaning a single unit, whereas Ibn Qutayba links it to tawatur, meaning continuity. On recitation, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it with tanwin, and the rest without it; al-Tabari prefers the reading without tanwin as the more eloquent, and holds both to be correct. On the word ahadith, al-Akhfash says it is used only for evil, while al-Qurtubi and others note that a good sense is also possible. As for the peoples meant, Ibn 'Abbas names the Children of Israel, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi mention Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, and others favour 'Ad and Thamud. Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb see in the verse above all a constant divine law against peoples who reject their prophets.

God says that He sent Moses and his brother Aaron with His signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they grew arrogant and were a people who dominated others through oppression. The commentators agree that the signs are miracles and that the clear authority is a proof that compels the opponent. Ibn Abbas lists the nine signs as the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the sea, the years of drought and the loss of fruits. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others note that the clear authority may refer to the staff, the mother of Moses' signs, to which many miracles are linked, such as its turning into a serpent that swallowed what the magicians had made. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi instead take the signs to be the miracles themselves and the authority to be the strength of their proof. Al-Hasan al-Basri understood the signs as the religious obligations. The word 'abidun is explained as obedient or humbled, since the Arabs called anyone who submitted to a king a worshipper of him. Pharaoh and his court refused to believe two men like themselves whose people served them; they denied the prophets and were drowned. On the next verse about the gift of the Book to Moses, many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan, hold that the pronoun refers to the Israelites, since the Torah was not given before Pharaoh's destruction.

This verse tells us that God sent Moses and his brother Aaron with His signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they reacted with arrogance because they were a domineering people. The commentators agree that the signs are the miracles, and that the clear authority is the evident proof. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy add that the staff may be meant, since it was the first and greatest of the miracles, while al-Razi lists several possible readings of the phrase. On the meaning of being domineering, al-Tabari explains it as oppression and dominance over the Children of Israel and others, al-Mawardi gives the senses of pride, polytheism and tyranny, and Ibn Kathir sees it as a refusal to submit. The chiefs then said they would not believe in two men like themselves, and that their own people were subservient to them; the scholars note that the Arabic word for worshippers can mean those who submit to a king. All agree that their denial led to their destruction by drowning. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi identify the Book given to Moses as the Torah, and most conclude that the pronoun in 'so that they may be guided' refers to the Children of Israel, since the Torah was revealed after Pharaoh's destruction.

The verse tells that Allah sent Moses and his brother Aaron with signs and clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs. They were arrogant and proud, dominating others through injustice. They then said, rejecting the message: shall we believe two men like us, when their people serve us? Most commentators understand the word ʿābidūn as meaning submissive, obedient and humbled. Abu ʿUbayda notes that the Arabs call anyone who submits to a king a servant of him, and this is why the people of al-Hira were called al-ʿibad. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd explain that Pharaoh wanted to keep himself and his chiefs above the Children of Israel, while al-Mawardi gives several meanings, including obedience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also mention that Pharaoh claimed divinity and so demanded worship from the people. All agree that their denial was the cause of their drowning. On the pronoun in the phrase so that they may be guided, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi hold that it refers to the Children of Israel, since the Torah was revealed after Pharaoh's people had been drowned, whereas al-Zamakhshari refers it to the family of Moses. On the signs, Ibn ʿAbbas identifies them as the nine signs, while al-Razi suggests that the clear authority may be the staff, the source of many miracles. Several commentators see in this objection the same argument used by earlier peoples, who held that a messenger had to be of a different nature from humans.

This verse closes the account of Pharaoh and his chiefs facing Moses and Aaron: they called the two prophets liars and were, as the commentators explain, destroyed by drowning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe how Pharaoh and his nobles grew arrogant before the proofs the two brought, and how they scornfully asked how they could believe two men like themselves, when their people were subject to them. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi explain that the word 'abidun here means submissive and humbled, since the Arabs called anyone who submitted to a king his worshipper.

The commentators broadly agree on the meaning of the verse's ending: the deniers were drowned, as al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud state. Al-Razi and al-Alusi note that the particle fa in "fakanu" marks that destruction was decreed after the denial, not that it followed immediately.

Opinions differ on other points. Regarding the "signs", Ibn 'Abbas identifies them as the nine signs, al-Hasan takes them to mean the religion, while al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari offer readings in which the "clear authority" refers to the staff or the hand. As for Pharaoh's claim, al-Zamakhshari notes that he presented himself as a deity and demanded worship from his people, which gives the word 'abidun a stronger sense than mere submission.

God says that He gave Moses the Book, the Torah, so that his people, the Children of Israel, might be guided by it and act upon its laws and admonitions. Most commentators agree that the pronoun in "that they may be guided" refers to the Children of Israel and not to Pharaoh and his people, since the Torah was revealed only after those people had been drowned, as Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud note. Ibn Kathir adds that after the Torah was revealed God no longer destroyed a nation wholesale, but commanded the believers to fight the disbelievers. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari, in one reading, take the sense to be "We gave the people of Moses the Book", a view others reject. Ibn Sa'di reports that Moses received the Torah after Pharaoh had been destroyed and the people of Israel delivered. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse completes the account of Moses' mission and prepares the lesson drawn from the peoples who rejected their prophets. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Atiyya read the word "perhaps" (la'alla) as an expression of hope attached to the Book. Al-Qurtubi notes that Moses alone is named because the Torah was sent down to him on the mount, with Aaron as his deputy among the people.

The commentators explain that God made the son of Mary and his mother a sign of His power, since Jesus was born without a father and Mary conceived him without a man touching her. Many treat this as one sign shared by both, while others hold that Jesus is a sign through the miracles performed by him and that his mother is a sign through bearing him without a husband. God then sheltered them on a raised ground, a rabwa, that offered a level, habitable place and flowing, visible water. On the location, opinions differ. Abu Hurayra identified it as ar-Ramla in Palestine, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Salam as the Ghouta of Damascus, Qatada and Ka'b as Jerusalem, and Ibn Zayd as Egypt. Ibn Kathir considers Jerusalem the most likely, since the Qur'an mentions it elsewhere, while al-Tabari argues that a place with visible flowing water does not fit ar-Ramla. For qarar, Ibn Abbas and others understand a level, spacious ground, while Qatada understands a place rich in fruit. Most read ma'in as flowing water visible to the eye, though its derivation is discussed between the root for eye and the root for benefit or abundance.

God addresses the messengers, telling them to eat from the good and lawful things and to do righteous deeds, for He knows fully what they do and will repay them. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the Prophet Muhammad alone, the plural being the Arabic way of addressing one person. Al-Tabari holds that Jesus, son of Mary, is addressed, citing the report that he ate from his mother's spun wool. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy explain that each messenger was addressed in his own time, so this is an ancient principle common to all of them, and Ibn Juzayy considers the reading that addresses Muhammad alone to be remote. On the meaning of the good things, some take them as what is lawful, others as what is pleasant and agreeable to eat; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi prefer the second in view of the context. Most commentators observe that placing lawful food before righteous deeds shows that good action requires lawful sustenance, and Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the man who raises his hands to heaven in supplication while his food is unlawful. Some also note that the same command was given to the believers in the Qur'an, so the rule applies to all.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the religion of the prophets is one in its foundations, and that the word umma here means the faith and the path. Al-Tabari links it to the preceding verses about lawful food and righteous deeds, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the address may be to all the messengers together or to Muhammad alone, expressed in the plural. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that this unity lies in the call to worship God alone. Al-Razi specifies that the agreement concerns knowledge of God and fear of Him, not the detailed laws, which may differ. Regarding the division described next, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as splitting into rival religions, while Ibn Kathir sees it as the disobedience of peoples who divided themselves. According to Qatada and Ibn Zayd, people scattered into different books, and the readings of the word zubur vary. The commentators also observe that reading the opening particle as inna or anna changes the grammar, Sibawayh attaching it to the end of the verse. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the phrase this community refers to the revealed law, which does not change. The verse closes with the command to fear God, the Lord of all.

The commentators explain that this verse describes what happened to earlier communities after they were commanded to unite around one religion: they split into many factions, each holding to a path it believed to be the truth. They differ on the meaning of "zuburan". Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean books: each group took up a scripture, believed in it and rejected the rest, or altered what it had. Mujahid and al-Sudi, followed by others, read it as pieces or sections, like fragments of iron, a reading al-Tabari also attributes to the Syrian reciters. Ibn Zayd holds that these books were their own invented writings and errors, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mention both the idea of altered books and that of inventions. The phrase "each faction rejoices in what it has" means that every group is pleased with its own belief and convinced it alone is right, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain. Ibn Ashur adds that this joy rested on habit rather than on evidence. The commentators disagree about who is addressed: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid take it to be the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, addressed in the plural, al-Tabari takes it to be Jesus, and al-Razi favours the Prophet. They agree that the verse warns against sectarianism and division in religion, and the following verses command the Prophet to leave these people in their error for a time.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ to leave the people of Quraysh in their error and confusion until the time of their punishment or their death, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. Most commentators take the word ghamra to mean a flood of water that covers a man's height, so the image is of people sunk in ignorance. The phrase "until a time" is understood in several ways: al-Sam'ani and Ibn Kathir take it to mean death, al-Razi adds the moment of seeing the truth or of punishment, and Ibn Juzayy and al-Mawardi mention the battle of Badr. Ibn Atiyya reports that some hold the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi treat it as a threat that stands. The next verse rejects the assumption that the wealth and children given to them are a sign of divine favour. Most exegetes explain that this is a respite and a gradual drawing-on, which they do not perceive. Al-Razi adds that these gifts may be given so that the proof falls more heavily upon them, and Ibn Kathir stresses that wealth without faith and righteous deeds proves nothing in one's favour.

This verse says that those immersed in their error imagine that the wealth and children God grants them in this life are a favour that hastens good for them, and the Qur'an rejects this assumption. The commentators read "We hasten for them the good things" as referring to giving and increasing, and to advancing good for them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur agree that this bounty is a respite and a lure: God gives them more so that they increase in sin, while they do not perceive it. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain "they do not perceive" as not knowing that it is a lure, while others take it as a threat. Ibn Kathir draws from it a warning to believers not to be dazzled by the worldly prosperity of others. Grammarians discuss how the clause introduced by "that" is built: al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari assume an omitted pronoun, al-Kisa'i holds that "innama" is a single particle needing no omission, and Ibn al-Anbari considers stopping at "and sons" to be an error. The commentators report these views without choosing between them. Some modern authors, such as al-Sha'rawi and Sayyid Qutb, connect the verse to the question of the apparent prosperity of unbelievers compared with the modest condition of believers.

This verse states that the wealth and children given to the disbelievers in this life are not a sign of God's approval nor an advance reward they have earned, according to the commentators in general. Al-Tabari and Mujahid explain that it is a respite and a gradual leading into ruin, which these people wrongly take for a favour. Ibn Kathir, who also cites Qatada, adds that God deceives them through their wealth and children, and that people should be judged not by their fortune but by their faith and righteous deeds.

Al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the passage as a rebuttal of the idea that these gifts are a mark of favour. Al-Nasafi draws from it an argument against the Mu'tazilites on the principle that God always does what is best for people. Commentators differ on the structure of the sentence: al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning 'we hasten for them by it', while Hisham held that the adverbial phrase 'in the good things' itself serves as the link. Al-Qurtubi records several readings, including 'we hasten' in the first person and 'it hastens' with the verb in the third person, attributed to al-Sulami and Ibn Abi Bakra.

Ibn Ashur explains that the question is one of rebuke, that the good things here are worldly goods, and that 'bal' corrects their assumption: they do not realise that this is only a lure toward destruction. Al-Jaza'iri concludes that for a people who have turned from God's religion, wealth is only a trial.

The commentators explain that this verse describes believers who fear the punishment of their Lord, a fear that goes together with obedience. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take ishfaq to mean fear, and hold that the believer combines good deeds with awe, as al-Hasan al-Basri reported. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya say that ishfaq is stronger than khashya, since it carries tenderness and a sharp expectation. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil take khashya here to mean punishment, while al-Razi understands it as constancy in obedience and eagerness to seek God's pleasure.

The commentators agree that the qualities that follow complete the picture: faith in God's signs, meaning the Qur'an and the creation that points to Him, and the rejection of associating partners. For al-Tabari and al-Razi this means sincerity in worship and freedom from showing off. Most understand "what they give" as charity, zakat and all acts of goodness, and Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr extend it to every pious deed, while others read "what they do", a reading attributed to Aisha.

The hadith of Aisha is the most cited explanation of the fearful heart: it concerns the one who prays, fasts and gives charity while fearing that his deeds will not be accepted. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim transmit it. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note the excellent order of these qualities, which leads to acting with fear, the rank of the truthful.

Finally, most exegetes conclude that these believers hasten toward good deeds. Some, like Ibn Abbas and Ibn Atiyya, add that this also means they receive benefits in this world, and al-Razi accepts both meanings.

This part of the verse describes believers who affirm the signs of their Lord, meaning they believe in them and act upon them. It follows the description of those who fear their Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand the signs as the revealed verses of the Book and its proofs, while al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani include both revealed signs and signs in creation. Al-Alusi adds that the signs include phenomena in the horizons and within the self. For al-Razi and al-Alusi, believing in the signs means assenting to what they indicate, not merely acknowledging that they exist. Ibn Kathir notes that this faith extends to God's decrees as well as His commands. Al-Razi observes that knowledge of God is gained through reflection and then shown by outward profession. Ibn Sa'di emphasises that hearing the verses increases faith and leads to contemplation. Ibn 'Ashur sees the signs as the proofs within the Qur'an, including its inimitability. Al-Sha'rawi links this quality to a warning against hidden shirk, which may affect even the believer. The commentators agree that this describes a steady faith expressed through action.

This verse describes one quality of the believers who race toward good deeds: they do not associate anyone with their Lord. The commentators explain that it means devoting worship to God alone. Al-Tabari says they make no partner with God in their worship, neither idol nor statue, and do not show off to any of His creatures. Al-Razi holds that the point is the hidden form of association, namely being sincere in worship so that one performs it only for the sake of God's face. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take it to cover both open and hidden association. Al-Nasafi restricts the reference to the polytheism of the Arabs of the time, while al-Biqa'i notes that a believer may be exposed to open or hidden association, and that the verse denies both. Al-Shawkani speaks of abandoning association entirely, outwardly and inwardly. Al-Alusi suggests the verse may also affirm the oneness of divinity after the oneness of lordship mentioned earlier, though most unbelievers acknowledge God's lordship. The verse is often read together with what follows, where the hadith of Aisha is cited about those who fast, pray and give charity while fearing their deeds will not be accepted. No commentator disputes this general meaning.

This verse describes believers who give what they have given, with hearts trembling in fear that it will not be accepted, knowing that they will return to their Lord to be judged. The commentators broadly agree that the giving means donating wealth in God's cause and that the trembling means fear. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr hold that it covers all acts of righteousness, while Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid restrict it to zakat and charity. Al-Hasan al-Basri says the believer combines good deeds with fear, whereas the hypocrite combines bad deeds with false security. The variant reading "ya'tuna ma ataw", attributed to 'A'isha, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, means doing what they did; several narrations from 'A'isha are cited to support it, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir consider the majority reading clearer. Al-Razi treats this quality as the fourth and highest stage, the station of the truthful. As for "they race to the good deeds and they are foremost in them", al-Tabari prefers Ibn 'Abbas's view that happiness was decreed for them in advance, while others read the preposition as meaning "toward" or "for their sake". The common thread is that righteous action and fear of falling short go together.

This verse describes those who hasten toward good deeds and outstrip others in them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi explain that they eagerly rush to acts of obedience, while al-Mawardi and al-Baydawi note that the phrase may also mean they gain worldly benefits and honour for good deeds in this life, a view Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi also give weight to. Opinions differ over the second clause, "wa hum laha sabiqun". Al-Tabari, quoting Ibn Abbas, takes it to mean that happiness was decreed for them by God in advance, which is why they hasten, and he prefers this reading because the particle "li" keeps its usual meaning. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, read it as "they go ahead toward them" or "they reach them before the Hereafter", and al-Qurtubi suggests they arrive first at the appointed times of prayer. For the qualities before this, most commentators agree that the fear and trembling of the heart in the verse refers to worry that one's deeds may not be accepted despite one's effort. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of Aisha, in which the Prophet explains that these are people who pray, fast and give charity while fearing their deeds will not be accepted, rather than those who commit sins. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari also mention a reading attributed to Aisha, "ya'tuna ma ataw", meaning they do what they do. Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Ashur emphasise the spiritual alertness and the healthy competition in goodness that follow from this attitude.

The verse states that God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, and that people's deeds are recorded with Him in a Book that speaks the truth, so no one is wronged. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand this Book as the Preserved Tablet or the registers of deeds kept by the recording angels, and see the verse as both a warning to wrongdoers and reassurance to the obedient. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the most apparent meaning is the register of deeds, though some read it as the Quran, and al-Qurtubi also prefers the register. On the notion of capacity, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi draw from it the rulings that the sick may pray seated and that one unable to fast may break the fast, while al-Razi and al-Nasafi stress that the verse refutes the idea that God imposes the impossible. Al-Razi further notes that the same principle is discussed at length in al-Baqara.

The following clause, 'but their hearts are in confusion about this', is read by most commentators, including Mujahid, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, as referring to the disbelievers, with 'this' meaning the Quran. Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya take the deeds mentioned afterwards to be sins committed apart from the truth. Al-Razi, following Abu Muslim, proposes instead that the passage describes the fearful believers, a view he considers preferable, though al-Alusi and others reject it. On the punishment that seizes the wealthy, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid refer it to the battle of Badr, al-Dahhak to famine, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Shawkani allow for punishment in the Hereafter, without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the description of the believers who fear their Lord. It states that the hearts of the disbelievers are submerged in a heedlessness that covers them from the Qur'an and the truth, and that they have evil deeds beyond what the believers are described as doing, which they carry on without respite. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi largely agree that the 'submersion' means a blindness or heedlessness toward the Qur'an, and that the 'deeds' are sins, polytheism and transgressions that they will commit and for which they will be punished. The reference of 'this' in 'from this' is disputed: Mujahid takes it as the Qur'an, Qatada as the Truth, and al-Zajjaj as the good deeds just mentioned or the book of deeds. For 'beyond that', Qatada and Mujahid speak of sins they must yet commit, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd of evil actions not yet done, and Ibn 'Abbas of evil deeds other than polytheism.
