Al-Razi judges the reading that connects the verse to the believers closer to the context, though he reports that Abu Muslim al-Isfahani took that line; al-Alusi finds it unconvincing, since the Qur'an never ascribes such submersion to the believers. Most exegetes read the phrase as a prediction of what they will do, with God granting them respite until they reach what has been decreed for them.

This verse describes the wealthy and privileged leaders of Quraysh, whose hearts are plunged in heedlessness of the Qur'an, and who still have evil deeds to commit before God seizes them with punishment. When the punishment strikes these pampered men, they cry out and plead, which is the meaning of the verb yajʼarun, a raised voice of distress like that of a bellowing bull. The commentators agree on this sense of the word. They differ on the nature of the punishment. Ibn ʻAbbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj understand it as the killing and capture at Badr, while al-Dahhak, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi also mention the famine that struck Mecca after the Prophet prayed against them. Al-Alusi, Ibn ʻAtiyya and Ibn ʻAshur, and al-Alusi reports that Ibn Taymiyya agreed, consider it more likely to be the punishment of the Hereafter, since the cry for help addressed to God is not answered there. The words "Do not cry out today; you will not be helped" are read by most as a rebuke that cuts off all hope, and al-Hasan takes them to mean that repentance will not be accepted at that point. Opinions differ on the referent of "bihi": the Sacred Mosque for most, the Qur'an or the Prophet for others. They also differ on "samiran tahjurun", where the verse refers to nightly gatherings around the Kaaba in which the Qur'an was mocked.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Quraysh when punishment overtakes them: they cry out and beg for help. They are then told, as a rebuke and to end all hope, not to cry out now, for they will not be helped against Our punishment and their clamour will profit them nothing. Nearly all agree that the word "ju'ar" means crying out, supplicating or wailing in distress, as Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Rabi' ibn Anas explain.

Opinions differ on which punishment is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj take it to be the slaughter by the sword at Badr, while Ibn al-Sa'ib, and in another report al-Dahhak, take it to be the famine that struck them after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against them. Al-Hasan and others point to the punishment of the Hereafter, and al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya combine both readings. The word "mutrafun" generally refers to the wealthy and powerful leaders.

On the verb "nakasa", some read it literally as turning back in flight from the recitation, others figuratively as turning away from the Qur'an. Regarding "mustakbirin bihi", Ibn Kathir and most commentators take the pronoun to refer to the Sacred House, in whose protection they boasted that no enemy could prevail over them, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya refer it to the Qur'an, so that their arrogance is a rejection of it. "Samir" means nightly conversation, and they gathered around the Ka'ba mocking the Qur'an as magic or poetry. The readings of "tahjurun" also differ: most read it as uttering vain talk or turning away from the truth, whereas Nafi' reads "tuhjirun", meaning uttering abuse, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Qutayba report.

Finally, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note that the command not to cry out may be a spoken address by the angels or a message conveyed by the situation itself.

In this verse God addresses the polytheists of Quraysh at the moment punishment strikes them: He forbids them to cry out for help, since they will not be given victory, and reminds them that the verses of the Qur'an were recited to them and that they turned their backs and fled from hearing them. The commentators agree that nukus means turning back, and that here it is a figure of speech for rejecting the truth. The meaning of 'mustakbirina bihi' is debated. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take the pronoun to refer to the sacred precinct, meaning they boasted of being its people and claimed no one could overcome them there. Ibn 'Atiyya and others take it to refer to the Qur'an, so their arrogance lay in rejecting it as soon as they heard it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi mention other possibilities, linking it to the Sacred House or to the verses. 'Samiran' is a circumstantial state and refers to people conversing at night, which Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain as Quraysh gathering around the Ka'ba to speak against the Qur'an. For 'tahjurun', the majority reading gives abandonment or raving, while Nafi's reading gives gross insult, which Ibn 'Abbas links to abuse of the Prophet and his companions. al-Tabari prefers the majority reading. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that some scholars drew from this verse a reproach of idle night gatherings.

In these verses God rebukes the Quraysh and tells them that their cries at the moment of punishment will not help them, since His verses were recited to them and they turned their backs and drew away, which is the meaning of nukus. The commentators agree that the verses are the Quran, that the cry (ju'ar) is a loud, pleading plea, and that the affluent (mutrafun) are the wealthy leaders struck by the punishment.

The meaning of "mustakbirina bihi" is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak, followed by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take the pronoun to refer to the Sacred Precinct or the House: they took pride in the Haram and claimed that no one could prevail over them as its people. Ibn Atiyya and a group read it as referring to the Quran, whose hearing breeds arrogance and rebellion. Mundhir ibn Sa'id takes it as referring to the Prophet, and al-Zamakhshari offers a close alternative.

Regarding "samiran", most take it as night gatherings around the Kaaba, with al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir adding that their talk was about the Quran and the Prophet. For "tahjurun", the reading with fatha and damma means turning away from the truth or talking nonsense according to Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari, while Nafi's reading with damma and kasra means uttering foul speech and insulting the Prophet.

All agree that these behaviours were the cause of the punishment, and that the verse rebukes people who rejected the truth after recognising it.

In this verse God rebukes the idolaters for failing to reflect on the Qur'an and for rejecting the Messenger ﷺ on the ground that he brings what their forefathers never received. Al-Tabari explains that the verse asks whether they did not ponder the revelation to grasp its lessons and proofs, and he notes that the particle 'am' may mean 'rather', so that they rejected it because it was unknown to their ancestors, a view also reported from Ibn Abbas. Al-Sam'ani, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir stress that messengers had been sent to earlier nations, from Noah to Abraham and Ismail, so the mission is no novelty. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir report another reading in which the fathers meant are Ismail and his descendants, who believed and obeyed. Several scholars, including al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur, add that God reminds them that they knew Muhammad's truthfulness and trustworthiness before his mission, which makes their denial unreasonable. As for the charge of madness, al-Baydawi and al-Razi note that they knew him to be the most sound-minded of men and that the accusation arose from his message opposing their desires. On the clause that most of them dislike the truth, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that some abstained out of fear of their people, as Abu Talib is said to have done, while al-Alusi and others read the phrase as applying to the whole group. Al-Razi, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi add that if the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted, and Ibn 'Ashur links these reproaches to their behaviour in the nightly gatherings around the Ka'ba.

In this verse God rebukes the idolaters for failing to recognise their messenger Muhammad ﷺ, though they knew his lineage, truthfulness and trustworthiness from his youth. The commentators read it as part of a series of rebukes: they did not reflect on the Qur'an, they wondered at a messenger coming when none had come to their fathers, they denied their messenger, and they called him mad. Most agree that Quraysh did know the Prophet before the mission and that their denial was stubbornness rather than ignorance. Ibn 'Abbas, Sufyan and Abu Salih are reported to say that they knew him but envied him, al-Nasafi speaks of rebellion and envy, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi recall their earlier recognition of his truthfulness. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn Sa'di point to his reputation before revelation, and al-Alusi cites Abu Talib's speech at the marriage to Khadija. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the rebuke concerns the rejection of his truthfulness rather than ignorance of his person. Al-Zamakhshari reads the negation as a rhetorical denial, while al-Sa'di and al-Biqa'i stress how false the accusation was. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the phrase 'their messenger' means he was one of them, which strengthens the reproach.

The commentators explain that this verse rejects the claim of the disbelievers that the Prophet ﷺ is possessed by madness. God says that he has brought them the truth, whose soundness no sensible person could miss, and that most of them dislike the truth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi attribute this dislike to envy, arrogance and blind adherence to the customs of their forefathers. Al-Tha'labi and al-Nasafi report that some of them did not hate the truth itself but refused it for fear of being reproached for abandoning their fathers' religion, as was the case with Abu Talib. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur note that the word "most" may refer to humankind in general or only to the Quraysh, and that this reading leaves room for those who were inclined toward the truth. Ibn Ashur adds that the truth here means the oneness of God, the resurrection and the laws revealed at Mecca. The verse belongs to a sequence of rebukes: neglect of reflection on the Qur'an, astonishment at a messenger sent without precedent, denial of the Prophet's known integrity before his mission, and finally the charge of madness. Al-Shinqiti recalls that earlier nations said the same to their messengers. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi stress that the Prophet's evident wisdom and sound judgement make the charge of madness untenable. The commentators give no legal rulings here; they focus on the meaning of the divine reproach and its context.

This verse states that if the truth had followed the desires of the disbelievers, the heavens, the earth and everyone in them would have been corrupted. The commentators differ on what "the truth" means. Most, including Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, Abu Salih and al-Suddi, take it to be God Himself: had He yielded to their wishes by sanctioning association, the order of the world would collapse. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj take it to be the Qur'an, which would have corrupted the world had it descended as they wished. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read "truth" as what is right and straight, with "following" as a metaphor, and argue that cosmic order rests on the true rather than on desire. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that human desires contradict one another, which would disrupt any governance of the universe.

On the phrase "We have brought them their reminder", opinions vary. Ibn 'Abbas explains it as the clarification of the truth, while al-Suddi, Sufyan, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as their honour and nobility, since the Prophet is one of them and the Qur'an is in their language. Others, such as Qatada, take it as a warning, or as the scripture they had wished for. Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi find the sense of honour the more evident, while the sense of admonition makes their rejection more severe. The verse ends by noting that they turn away from this reminder.

The commentators also discuss the words "kharj" and "kharaj", which Abu 'Amr distinguishes: the first is what one gives voluntarily, the second what is owed. The Prophet therefore asks them for no payment, and the reward of his Lord is better.

This verse tells the Prophet that he does not ask people for a payment for his message, and that what his Lord gives him, whether provision in this life or reward in the next, is better, because God is the best of providers. Commentators agree that the Prophet asked no wage, and that the question is a rebuke to those who turned away from him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand the better portion as lasting reward in the hereafter, while al-Kalbi, cited by Abu Hayyan, and Abu al-Su'ud take it as provision in this world, and al-Hasan as the reward of the hereafter. Al-Baydawi keeps both options open: provision in this life or recompense in the next. Al-Jubba'i, cited by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, draws from the closing phrase that no creature can equal God's bounty, and that people can also provide for one another.

On the words kharj and kharaj the scholars differ. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala, reported by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi, holds that kharaj is what is owed while kharj is what is given freely, and al-Zamakhshari sees kharj as the narrower term. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya treat the two as essentially the same, Ibn Atiyya noting only a difference in usage. The readings vary: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read kharajan, Ibn Amir reads kharjan in both places, and the rest read kharjan followed by kharaj.

Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan link the passage to the years of famine that struck Quraysh and to Abu Sufyan's appeal to the Prophet for relief.

This part of the verse says that the Prophet ﷺ calls the idolaters to the straight path, which the commentators identify as Islam, a path without any crookedness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the verse together with what precedes it: the Prophet asks no wage for his message, so his call should be accepted. Al-Zamakhshari adds that he was well known for his honesty among his people, that he was neither mad nor greedy, and that he called only to Islam, while exposing their flaws, chiefly their neglect of reflection. Al-Qurtubi notes that the path is called a way because it leads to Paradise. Al-Baydawi says that sound minds bear witness to its straightness. As for the next verse, most commentators read it as saying that those who do not believe in the Hereafter deviate from this path. Ibn Abbas and al-Tabari take the word nakibun to mean those who turn aside, while Qatada reads it as those who are confused, al-Hasan as those who abandon it, and al-Kalbi as those who turn away. These meanings are close to one another. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that the deviation stems from disbelief in the resurrection, since one who hopes for no reward and fears no punishment will not follow this way. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud likewise present this as the decisive argument that leaves the opponents without excuse.

The commentators explain that this verse describes those who do not believe in the Hereafter as deviating from the straight path, which is the religion of Islam. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan explained the word "nakibun" as deviating, inclining away, abandoning or turning aside, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya noted that these meanings are close. Several, such as al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, hold that belief in the Hereafter is the strongest motive for seeking the truth, so denying it leads to straying.

Al-Zamakhshari sees these verses as closing the argument against the polytheists and removing their excuses, since the Prophet was known for his integrity and asked for no wealth. Al-Alusi suggests that "the path" may refer to the path in general, which better shows how far they have gone astray, while al-Shinqiti takes it as the straight path leading to Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the passage to the famine that struck the Quraysh after the Prophet's supplication, recounting through Ibn 'Abbas how Abu Sufyan came to plead with him after they had eaten the leather-and-blood food called al-'ilhiz.

The commentators differ on the "harm" mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj understood it as hunger and drought, while al-Razi lists hunger, killing and captivity, or the punishment of the Hereafter. According to them, if God removed the harm, they would persist in their rebellion and remain bewildered in their error, as the word "ya'mahun" describes.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of those who do not believe in the Hereafter. Even if God were merciful to them and removed the harm that afflicted them, such as famine and hardship, they would persist in their rebellion and wander confused in their error. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Juraij take the harm to be the hunger that struck the Quraysh, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ invoked a drought upon them, so that they ate al-'ilhiz and Abu Sufyan came to ask him for relief. Some accounts add that Thumama ibn Uthal had cut off their grain supplies from Yamama.

There is broad agreement on the meanings of the key words: lajaj is obstinate persistence, tughyan is excess in disbelief and arrogance, and 'amah is wandering in confusion. Al-Zamakhshari explains istikana as moving from one state to another, while others derive it from the root sakana, and grammarians debate the point. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas that every occurrence of 'law' refers to what will never happen.

Opinions differ on the nature of the harm and on the verse that follows. Al-Razi offers three readings: hunger and worldly harms, killing and captivity, or the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn Juzayy judges that the 'gate of severe punishment' refers to the punishment of the Hereafter and considers it the most likely, while others identify it with the battle of Badr or the famine. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the threat of punishment that precedes it and notes that the past tense here refers to the future.

This verse says that God afflicted the polytheists with hardship, namely famine and the killing of their leaders by the sword at Badr, yet they neither humbled themselves before their Lord nor implored Him, and remained stubborn. Most commentators understand the punishment as the famine that struck Quraysh after the Prophet invoked God against them, seven years like the years of Joseph; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate the account of Abu Sufyan coming to plead with the Prophet, and al-Tabari says the verse was revealed on that occasion. Ibn Abbas, al-Asamm and others take it to mean the killing and capture at Badr, while al-Hasan refers to earlier nations. The gate of severe punishment is understood by Ibn Abbas and most scholars as the battle of Badr, by Muqatil and al-Tabari as hunger, and by al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur as the punishment of the Hereafter; al-Razi explains that ibsal means despair of all good. On the word istakanu, al-Zamakhshari and most read it as from kawn, to move from one state to another, while some take it from sukun with a lengthened vowel; Ibn Ashur finds the latter weak. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that the verse blames those who do not turn to God in hardship, and Ibn al-Qayyim adds that God loves to be complained to. The commentators agree that the verse shows the hardness of the disbelievers' hearts and their persistence in denial.

The commentators explain that the verse describes disbelievers who neither humbled themselves before their Lord nor implored Him, neither under mercy nor under hardship. When a gate of severe punishment was opened upon them, they were left in despair and bewilderment. They differ on what this punishment was. Ibn 'Abbas, followed by Ibn Jurayj, al-Baghawi and al-Samarqandi, identifies it as the killing at Badr. Mujahid, Muqatil, al-Suddi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify it as the famine that the Prophet ﷺ invoked upon Quraysh, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour this view, citing the report of Abu Sufyan. Others, including al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, point to death, the Hour, or the Fire in the Hereafter, and Ibn Juzayy prefers the Hereafter because its hardship is greater. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi favour the famine, which they regard as harsher than captivity or killing. Ibn 'Atiyya sees the punishment as an unspecified threat. On the word istakana, al-Zamakhshari derives it from kawn, while others derive it from sukun. Nearly all agree that iblas means despair of every good.

This verse states that God created for you hearing, sight and hearts, meaning the faculties of understanding by which one reasons, and that gratitude for these blessings is scant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that these faculties were given so that people might hear, see and understand, and that they hardly give thanks for them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi stress that these organs are singled out because religious and worldly benefits depend on them, and that whoever does not use them for their purpose is like someone who lacks them. Al-Razi also reports the view of Abu Muslim that the verse rebukes the ingrate disbeliever, meaning that they hardly give thanks at all rather than that they give some small measure of it. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that true gratitude consists in using these faculties for their purpose and submitting to the Giver without associating anything with Him. On the phrase qalilan ma tashkurun, most commentators read it as near-total absence of gratitude, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as genuine but scant thanks. The following verses, on creation, resurrection and the alternation of night and day, are offered as evidence calling for reflection. Several commentators also note that the Meccan deniers of resurrection dismissed it as the fables of the ancients.

The commentators explain that this verse states that God is the One who created you and scattered you across the earth, and that to Him you will be gathered. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi render the word dhara'a as creating or dispersing, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as multiplying and populating the earth. They agree that the gathering (hashr) means the assembling of people for judgment and recompense after resurrection.

The verse belongs to an argument for resurrection: the One who created humans at the beginning can create them again. Al-Razi notes that the passage answers those who thought it impossible for bones reduced to dust to be raised. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi connect this reply to the unbelievers' rejection of the messengers, whom they dismissed as tales of the ancients.

The main disagreement concerns the phrase fi al-ard. Al-Kalbi and Yahya ibn Sallam take it to mean creation, Ibn Shajara takes it to mean dispersal, and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani understands it as spreading people through reproduction until they multiply. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the phrase "to Him" implies an unstated object, namely "to His judgment and decree". Al-Zamakhshari stresses that the mention of dispersal recalls the separation that precedes the final gathering.

Modern commentators such as al-Sha'rawi emphasise the wisdom in spreading people across the whole earth, and the point that the God who scatters can also gather.

The commentators explain that this verse states that God alone gives life and causes death, and that the alternation and variation of night and day belong to Him. Al-Tabari understands giving life as breathing the spirit into the drop after its stages, followed by death. Al-Farra', al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain the difference of night and day as their succession and their contrast in darkness and light, or as one growing while the other shrinks. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi stress their alternating succession, and Ibn 'Atiyya allows the sense of clear contrast as well.

Most exegetes agree that the question "will you not then reason?" invites reflection: whoever creates and causes death is able to resurrect, and this is the core argument for the afterlife. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Sa'di connect the verse to the blessings listed just before it, hearing, sight and the heart, which people rarely thank God for, and to the creation on earth and the final gathering. Al-Zamakhshari explains that hearing, sight and hearts are mentioned because religious and worldly benefits depend on them.

The scholars differ on a reading point: Abu 'Amr and others read "ya'qilun" in the third person, which Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi connect to a shift of address, while others see it as addressed to believers. As for the disbelievers, the tafsirs report that they respond with denial, like their predecessors, judging resurrection impossible.

This verse describes how the Meccan unbelievers did not benefit from the signs that show God's power, and instead repeated the words of earlier peoples who denied the resurrection. According to the commentators, they said in disbelief and astonishment: 'When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we really be raised?' The word 'bal' marks a shift from the argument based on God's favours to a description of how they responded to these signs. The exegetes agree that the verse refers to the deniers of resurrection among the Quraysh, who followed the attitude of their predecessors; Ibn 'Atiyya suggests the peoples such as 'Ad and Thamud. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Sa'di report that this denial rests on the belief that re-creation after annihilation is impossible, and that their phrase 'these are only the fables of the ancients' means that what the Prophet says about resurrection is merely written stories without reality. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud extend the reproach to unbelievers in general who follow the same path. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verses combine the argument from God's power over the ordering of the world with the proof of resurrection, and that placing 'lahu' before 'ikhtilaf al-layl wa al-nahar' implies exclusivity. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan record differences of reading in the following reply, 'li-Llah' versus 'Allah', which they agree do not change the meaning. Taken together, the verse affirms belief in resurrection and warns against blind imitation.

This verse reports the words of those who deny resurrection: when we are dead and have become dust and bones, will we really be raised? The commentators read it as an expression of astonishment that treats the idea as impossible. Al-Tabari says they repeated what their predecessors had said and did not learn from the proofs of God's power, while al-Razi notes that they rejected resurrection by blindly following their forefathers. Ibn Kathir reports that they found the restoration of decayed bones unthinkable. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi describe the tone as denial and wonder, and al-Baydawi adds that they did not consider that they had been dust before being created. Ibn Ashur explains that the verse connects with what precedes it by comparing them to earlier peoples, and that mentioning death, dust and bones strengthens the denial. Nearly all the commentators agree that the verses that follow answer them by pointing to God's power to give life and cause death, and to his creation of hearing, sight and hearts. They differ on the phrase 'fables of the ancients': al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean what the ancients wrote that has no reality, while al-Baydawi sees it as their lies. On recitation, most readers pronounce two hamzas, while Ibn 'Amir reads one in the form of a statement. Many commentators treat this passage as a response not only to idolaters but to those who deny life after death.

This verse reports the words of those who deny resurrection: we and our fathers were promised this before, but we have never seen it, and it is nothing but the fables of the ancients. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that they reject what earlier messengers announced about resurrection, and find it hard to believe. Ibn Kathir adds that they took this belief from the books of earlier peoples. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi explain that the word asatir is the plural of ustura, meaning what the ancients wrote that has no reality, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi consider this the more sound meaning. Others derive it from satr, plural asfar, then asatir. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link these words to the preceding context, in which people reject the afterlife by imitating their forefathers, and al-Razi notes that they assumed resurrection would happen in this world. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi connect their denial to reasoning from the fate of earlier nations such as 'Ad and Thamud. The commentators go on to argue that God's lordship over the earth, the heavens and the Throne shows that He can resurrect. Al-Razi also draws from this the prohibition of idol worship. On the recitation, al-Tabari judges that both readings are close in meaning and both are acceptable. Al-Sha'rawi regards the claim as sophistry, since the resurrection has not yet come at its appointed time.

God commands His Prophet to ask the polytheists who deny the resurrection: to whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know? The commentators agree that the answer they cannot avoid is that it belongs to God alone, since reason acknowledges Him as its creator and owner, and that the question mocks their ignorance and rebukes them. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy read it as an argument against those who deny resurrection: whoever created the earth at the beginning can recreate it. Al-Razi adds that it may also refute idolaters who acknowledged God yet worshipped others alongside Him. Questions follow about the Lord of the seven heavens and the mighty Throne, and about who holds the dominion of all things, and the answer is always God, which leads to successive rebukes: will you not reflect, will you not fear Him, how are you bewitched. The readings differ over the lam: Abu 'Amr and the Iraqi readers say «Allah» in the nominative in the last two instances, following the form of the question, while the others say «li-Llah» in the genitive, following its meaning. Al-Tabari considers both acceptable while preferring the majority reading, which matches the script of the mushafs. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri report that the Arabs knew that one who grants protection cannot be overridden, meaning God protects whom He wills and no one can protect against Him. Al-Zamakhshari sees contempt and a charge of ignorance in the phrasing, and al-Shawkani supplies an omitted apodosis after the condition: then tell me. The commentaries close by exalting God above offspring and partners, and by affirming that knowledge of the unseen and the seen belongs to Him alone.

This passage from Surat al-Mu'minun gives an argument that God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to put to the Meccans who deny the Resurrection. He asks them whose the earth and its inhabitants are, and they will inevitably answer: 'To God.' He then says: 'Will you not then take heed?' meaning that they should reflect and recognise that the One who created these things in the first place can also bring creation back after death. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain that this admission is forced upon them by natural reason, and that the question serves as rebuke and a call to remember. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the truth is self-evident and needs only brief reflection. The reciters differ on whether the answer reads 'lillah' or 'Allah' in the two following occurrences: Abu 'Amr and the Iraqi readers give the answer as the literal question requires, while the majority use the particle lam, following the meaning of the question. Al-Tabari considers both readings valid and close in meaning, and al-Razi says they do not differ in sense. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri, stress that the verse calls for abandoning the worship of anyone other than the Creator. All agree that the passage belongs to the argument for God's oneness and His power to resurrect, and that the question is both rebuke and an invitation to reflection.

God commands His Prophet to ask the polytheists who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne. They will answer that it all belongs to God, and the Prophet then rebukes them for not fearing Him and for associating others with Him. The commentators explain that mentioning the seven heavens and the Throne shows that the owner and disposer of the greatest creatures is God, which makes their associating partners with Him absurd. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the Meccans acknowledged God as Creator and Owner, yet worshipped idols so that these would bring them closer to Him. Ibn Kathir regards the Throne as the greatest of creations, encompassing the heavens and the earth, and cites several reports from the early scholars about its magnitude. Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi note a difference in recitation: Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read the word for God without the preposition lam, following the wording of the question, while the majority read it with lam, following its meaning. They consider both readings valid and close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the answer with lam refers to ownership, which they judge more precise, and Ibn 'Ashur adds that the polytheists avoided saying the Lord of the heavens is God, since they had given the angels a divine role. Al-Razi offers several ways to understand the argument: the One who created the earth and its inhabitants can raise them again, and the One who holds all things and protects without being protected alone deserves worship. The commentators explain the phrase 'how then are you deluded' as meaning how are you turned away from the truth, and some identify the deceiver as Satan or passion.

God commands His Prophet to ask the polytheists who owns the earth and those in it, then who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the mighty Throne. They will answer that it all belongs to God, and he rebukes them: will you not then fear God? That is, will you not fear His punishment by worshipping others besides Him? The commentators broadly agree on this: the idolaters acknowledge God's lordship, and that acknowledgment should lead them to affirm His oneness and belief in the Resurrection. Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and Ibn Sa'di explain the question in these terms. Al-Tabari understands taqwa here as fear of punishment for disbelief and for denying the Messenger. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi suggest the address may target those who deny the Resurrection or the worshippers of idols. On the recitation, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read Allah without the lam, following the literal wording, while the majority read li-Llah with the lam, following the sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi regard both readings as valid and close in meaning, and al-Tabari prefers the majority reading because it matches the script of the codices. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that mentioning the Lord in the question implies a question about ownership, hence the lam. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the polytheists avoided saying that God is Lord of the heavens, since they worshipped angels, and so they were content to admit that He owns them. The commentators agree that the verse argues from what they already admit, and that the rebuke moves from the call to reflect, to pious fear, and then to deception, that is, being turned away from the truth.

God instructs His Prophet to ask the polytheists: in whose hand is the dominion of everything, that is, its sovereignty and treasuries? He grants protection to whom He wills, and no one can protect against Him whoever He wants to punish. Mujahid explains malakut as the treasuries of everything, whereas al-Dahhak, al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi understand it as sovereignty, the added ta' giving emphasis as in jabarut and rahabut. As for ijara, most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean protection, aid or preventing harm: God protects whom He wills, and none can protect anyone against Him. Al-Mawardi offers two readings, in this world where no one can prevent the ruin God intends or stop the victory He grants, and in the hereafter where no one can deprive a deserving person of reward or rescue one deserving punishment; al-Qurtubi regards both as valid. On the expected answer, all agree that the pagans will acknowledge that sovereignty belongs to God. Regarding fa-anna tusharun, al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas read it as 'you are lying', al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi as 'you are turned away from belief in resurrection' or 'falsehood appears to you as truth', and al-Zamakhshari as a metaphor for deception that diverts from the truth. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi, note that the verse turns the pagans' own acknowledgment of God's lordship against their idolatry.

God commands His Prophet to ask the polytheists to whom belongs the dominion over all things. Mujahid and al-Dahhak explain malakut as the treasuries or the sovereignty of everything, and the verse adds that God gives protection to whom He wills while no one can protect anyone against Him. Since they can only answer that it belongs to God, the Prophet asks: how then are you deluded? Ibn Abbas takes the word tusharun to mean that you lie, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as being deceived and turned away from right guidance, and al-Zamakhshari names the deceiver as Satan and desire. Al-Tabari defines magic as making something appear to the viewer otherwise than it really is, so the meaning becomes how the false is made to seem true to you. Al-Razi reads the verses as a proof against those who deny resurrection and against idol worshippers alike. Most commentators agree that the Arabs acknowledged God's lordship, and that the rebuke targets the contradiction between that acknowledgment and worshipping others or denying the resurrection. On the recitation, Abu Amr and Ya'qub drop the lam in Allah to follow the wording of the question, while the rest keep it to follow its meaning; Ibn Kathir and al-Razi hold that this does not change the sense. Ibn Ashur sees the question as expressing astonishment and takes magic here as the spreading of falsehood by the leaders of disbelief.

This verse states that God has brought the idolaters the truth, namely the monotheism and Islam with which He sent His Prophet ﷺ, and that their claims of a divine son and a divine partner are false. Al-Tabari explains that the truth means the certain religion, and he notes that these polytheists lied when they claimed the angels are God's daughters. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di understand the truth as the clear proofs and revelation, and Ibn Sa'di adds that it includes justice in commands and prohibitions. The commentators agree on a rational argument: if there were several gods, each would withdraw with what he created and the stronger would overpower the weaker, which would destroy the order of the world. Ibn Sa'di draws from the harmony of the cosmos a proof of God's oneness. Al-Razi links the verse to the earlier arguments about resurrection and idol worship. On the reading, most read 'alimi in the genitive as an epithet of God, while Nafi' and the Kufans read it in the nominative as a new sentence; al-Tabari prefers the nominative, and Ibn 'Atiyya finds it the more eloquent. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a rebuttal of the charge that the Prophet was bewitched. Several scholars, including al-Shawkani and al-Alusi, note that the verse concerns both monotheism and the resurrection.

This verse states that God has taken no son and that no god exists alongside Him, and it rejects the claims of the idolaters. The commentators explain the argument by reductio: if there were several gods, each would take what he created and withdraw his rule, and they would contend for supremacy as earthly kings do, so the order of the cosmos would collapse. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir present this as a refutation of those who called the angels God's daughters and of those who worshipped idols. Several theologians rest the argument on mutual hindrance, which Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir set out, while Ibn Juzayy argues that the verse gives a different proof based on the interconnection of creation, and Ibn 'Ashur calls it a demonstrative argument, whereas al-Alusi regards it as a persuasive one. On the reading of 'Alimi al-ghayb, al-Akhfash prefers the genitive so the sentence stays in one line, while Abu 'Ali and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the nominative, and al-Tabari chooses it too. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the son is denied before the partner because the angel-worshippers were the more persuasive error. Ibn Sa'di draws from the regular motion of the sun, moon and stars the evidence of one God, and all agree that God's knowledge of the unseen and the seen excludes any associate.

In this verse God declares Himself exalted above having a son or a partner. The commentators explain that the verse affirms God has taken no son and that no god exists alongside Him, and that the claims of the polytheists are false. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir rely on the rational argument that if there were several gods, each would be alone in possessing what he created, the stronger would overpower the weaker, and the order of the universe would collapse. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the coherent and harmonious order of the cosmos as evidence of the unity of its Creator, and Ibn Sa'di illustrates this with the movement of the sun, the moon and the stars.

As for "Knower of the unseen and the seen", the commentators explain that God knows what is hidden from His creatures and what they witness, and that His knowledge encompasses everything. That is why the verse continues with "Exalted is He above what they associate with Him", meaning He is glorified and far above any partner. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi see in this knowledge a further proof of the absence of a partner, since a partner could not comprehend what the other created. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others favour the nominative reading as the clearest, while al-Akhfash considers the genitive better for the unity of the sentence.

The commentators differ on the target of "He has taken no son": some see it as a refutation of those who said the angels are God's daughters, others as a refutation of Christians and dualists. Some hold that the forgiving verse that follows was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others consider it still binding among Muslims.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to make this supplication: My Lord, if You are to show me the punishment they are promised, do not place me among the wrongdoing people, that is, do not let me perish with them but save me from their fate. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that this is an expression of humility and submission, since the Prophet was protected from harm, and Ibn Kathir links it to a hadith transmitted by Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi report that al-Hasan al-Basri said God had informed His Prophet of a vengeance that would fall on his community without telling him when. The commentators agree that this punishment concerns this world, that God is able to inflict it, and that it came to pass at Badr or at the conquest of Mecca according to Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi, while Ibn Ashur also sees a reference to the Hereafter. God then commands repelling evil with what is better. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record several views: forgiveness and forbearance according to al-Hasan, greeting according to Ata and al-Dahhak, exhortation, or answering idolatry with monotheism. Ibn Atiyya holds that this ruling on morality remains valid but that its application to the peace treaties with unbelievers was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi and al-Nasafi consider it binding on the community as long as it does not compromise the religion. Finally God commands seeking refuge from the promptings (hamazat) of the devils, which the commentators understand as their incitements and whisperings, Ibn Zayd seeing madness in them, and from their presence in all one's affairs, according to Ibn Kathir.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to ask his Lord to deliver him from the punishment of the wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists, should He show him its fulfilment, and not to place him among them so that he perishes with them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the request as seeking safety and a place among those whom God is pleased with, while al-Zajjaj understands it as being kept outside that group. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi report, through a narration attributed to al-Hasan, that God had told the Prophet of a vengeance awaiting his community without specifying when, so he was taught this supplication. Al-Zamakhshari answers the objection about a sinless prophet asking such a thing by saying that a servant may ask for what he knows will not happen, to show humility, and cites the Prophet's frequent seeking of forgiveness. Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi note that repeating the word Lord intensifies the entreaty.

Regarding the promise that God is able to show the Prophet what He threatens, al-Tabari sees it as God's power to hasten the punishment, which He delays until the appointed term. Ibn Kathir reports that most scholars take it as a worldly punishment such as the battle of Badr, while others mention the conquest of Mecca or punishment in the Hereafter.

On repelling evil with what is better, al-Hasan explains it as forbearance and pardon, Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak as greeting with peace, and Ibn Shajara as wiping out evil with good. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention admonition and sincere advice. Some hold the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others consider it still binding, since conciliation is encouraged as long as it does not harm religion or dignity. On the whisperings of the devils, Ibn Zayd takes them to mean madness, while others understand them as incitements to sin. Seeking refuge from their presence is explained by al-Kalbi as applying during Qur'an recitation and by most scholars as applying in all circumstances.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a supplication Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to make: asking his Lord for safety from punishment should he be shown the torment threatened against the disbelievers. The verse then affirms that God is able to show him what He has promised them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God can indeed bring this punishment, but delays it for a wisdom, namely so that the Book reaches its appointed term. Al-Tabari notes that the disbelievers denied the threat and mocked it, and the verse answers them. The commentators differ on when this punishment occurred. Ibn Abbas and others, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, place it at Badr or the conquest of Mecca, while Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud speak of punishment in the Hereafter. Abu al-Su'ud judges the more likely reading to be a total destruction that would not be manifested through the Prophet. Al-Razi keeps both possibilities open, while Ibn Ashur holds it is a worldly punishment fulfilled at Badr. On the following verse, which commands repelling evil with what is better, the scholars largely agree it means forgiveness, overlooking offences and patience. Al-Hasan and Mujahid take it as restraint of anger and greeting, while al-Zamakhshari understands it as pardon combined with the greatest possible kindness. On whether it is abrogated by the verse of the sword, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya hold that it is, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Ashur consider it still valid so long as conciliation does not compromise the religion.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to meet the evil of the polytheists with the best response: forgiveness, forbearance and patience under abuse, leaving their fate to God, who knows best what they say about Him and about him. The commentators give several meanings to this 'best'. Al-Hasan al-Basri understands it as pardoning and overlooking the offender; Mujahid, al-Dahhak and 'Ata' take it as greeting the offender with peace in response to insult; Ibn 'Abbas takes it as the testimony that there is no god but God, the evil being polytheism. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi also report that repelling wrongdoing may be done through admonition. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the comparative form is stronger than saying 'with good', since the aim is to answer evil with the greatest good possible. Opinions differ on whether the rule still applies. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword with regard to unbelievers, but remains valid among believers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi report this view too, but also say it is not abrogated, since conciliation is commended as long as it does not lead to harm to the religion or to one's dignity. Ibn Juzayy sees a command of pardon and good character that is not abrogated. Several commentators link to this passage the request for refuge from the whisperings (hamazat) of the devils and from their presence in all affairs, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect especially with prayer and the recitation of the Qur'an.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to seek refuge in Him from the goadings and whisperings of the devils, and to ask Him for protection from their presence in all his affairs. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid explain the "hamazat" as promptings, whisperings, puffing and spitting, while Ibn Zayd takes them as strangling and others as madness. As for their "presence," most commentators understand it as presence in every circumstance, though al-Kalbi and Ibn 'Abbas restrict it to the recitation of the Quran, al-Kalbi also to prayer, and 'Ikrima to the moment of death.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the root meaning is a prod, like the spur a horse-trainer uses to make a mount move, so the devils urge people toward disobedience. Al-Nasafi repeats this image. Ibn 'Ashur suggests that the "devils" here may mean the Quraysh opponents who harassed the Prophet, while most commentators keep the sense of unseen jinn.

Many commentators connect this verse to the preceding command to repel evil with what is better. Ibn Kathir sees in it a remedy for dealing with people, and al-Hasan holds that only one who controls his anger can attain this virtue. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain this command as forgiveness, greeting or admonition, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that some held its tolerant aspect abrogated by the verse of fighting. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur link this request for protection to the strength the Prophet needed to forgive.

In this verse the Prophet asks God to protect him from the presence of the devils near him. Ibn Zayd says it refers to their presence in any of his affairs, al-Kalbi says it means their presence during the recitation of the Quran, and Ikrima says it means their presence at the moment of death. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain that the devil comes only to incite evil, so seeking refuge from his presence means seeking refuge from his harm.

The verse follows the command to repel evil with what is better, by forgiving and showing kindness, and to leave the fate of the wrongdoers to God, who knows what they say. Al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di present this as a way of resisting Satan, who is not turned away by kindness. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the harm caused by the jinn from the harm caused by hostile people, and holds that seeking protection guards against both.

The commentators agree on the general sense of seeking protection from the evil the devils whisper. They differ on how broad the feared presence is. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir apply it to all of life's circumstances, while al-Mawardi reports that most scholars take it this way and others restrict it to prayer or to the moment of death. Ibn Kathir also cites an invocation taught by the Prophet for sleep, and al-Qurtubi relates the verse to the Prophet's supplication against whispering devils.

This verse describes a disbeliever at the moment of death, who sees what awaits him and begs to be sent back to the world to do the righteous deeds he neglected. The commentators agree that this plea will not be granted, and that the word "kallā" that follows is a rebuke and a rejection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that regret overtakes him and his request is in vain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi add that his words are empty: he will keep repeating them out of remorse, and even if he were returned he would not keep his word, as another verse says of those sent back to what they had been forbidden.

The plural form "irji'ūnī" is debated. Most read it as a form of honour toward God, as one addresses kings, and cite poetic examples. Others, such as Ibn Jurayj and al-Tha'alibi, take it as a cry to God followed by an address to the angels, while al-Mazini sees it as a repetition of the request.

As for the "barzakh" behind them, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd understand it as a barrier between death and resurrection, al-Dahhak as the space between this world and the hereafter, Qatada as the rest of the worldly life, and al-Kalbi as the interval between the two blasts of the trumpet, said to be forty years. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that these views converge: there is no return to the life of this world.

This verse describes a person at the moment of death who, seeing what awaits him, regrets his neglect and begs to be returned to the world to do righteous deeds in what he left behind. The commentators agree that this plea will not be granted: the word "kallā" is a rebuke and a rejection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the return as a return to the life of this world, and Ibn Kathir links the passage to other verses where the disbelievers ask for a return. On the meaning of "what I have left", opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as faith, monotheism, or obedience that was neglected, while others, including al-Qurtubi and one of al-Razi's options, take it as wealth that could be given in charity. Al-Razi nevertheless considers the broader sense, covering every duty neglected in worship and rights, the more likely. On the phrase "a word he says", al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that he will inevitably utter it under the weight of remorse, whereas Ibn Juzayy and al-Sa'di see it as mere words with no sincerity or benefit. As for the barzakh, Mujahid understands it as a barrier between death and the return to the world, Dahhak and Ibn Zayd as the interval between death and resurrection, Qatada as the remainder of worldly life, and al-Kalbi as the period between the two blasts of the trumpet. Finally, al-Qurtubi and others read the plural "irji'ūnī" as a mark of honour toward God, while some take it as a repetition of the appeal.

The verse describes the moment when the Trumpet is blown: on that day there will be no kinship ties that benefit anyone, and no one will ask another about his state, each being absorbed in his own fate. The commentators agree on this general meaning, but differ on which blast is meant. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Mas'ud that it is the second blast, the one of resurrection, while others, including Ibn Abbas in one of his reports, al-Sam'ani, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, identify it as the first, the blast that causes all living beings to swoon. Regarding the negation of kinship, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain it as the cutting of ties of affection and mutual help, while kinship itself remains, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy understand it as the disappearance of its effects. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as the absence of support and intercession. On the question of mutual questioning, many commentators, among them al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, explain that it is absent during moments of terror and present at other times, which reconciles it with the verse in as-Saffat where people do ask one another. Al-Sha'rawi and al-Shinqiti also note that the affirmation and the denial concern different situations, not a contradiction. Several commentators, such as Ibn Juzayy and al-Baghawi, link the verse to the words of the unbelievers asking to be returned to the world, and to the weighing of deeds that follows.

This verse states that whoever's good deeds outweigh his bad on the Day of Judgment is the successful one who is saved, while whoever's scale is light is the loser who will remain forever in Hell. Ibn 'Abbas, followed by Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, explains the scales as the weighed deeds that have value before God, and al-Baydawi adds that they include both beliefs and actions. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi describe a real instrument with two pans and a tongue, on which good deeds appear in their finest form and bad ones in their ugliest, though al-Razi also notes that the term may be a metaphor for justice. Al-Tabari understands the 'falah' as eternal dwelling in the gardens of bliss, while most others take it as success and deliverance from the Fire. As for the loss, the commentators see it as the failure of those who squandered their souls and forfeited their share of God's mercy.

The exegetes then describe the punishment in the following verse. Ibn 'Abbas explains 'talfahu' as burning and consuming, and the commentators define 'kulūh' as the drawing back of the lips that exposes the teeth, illustrated by a verse of al-A'sha and by hadiths reported by Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi. Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb see in this a concrete image that makes an abstract idea accessible to everyone. There is agreement that this torment targets the disbelievers, while Ibn Sa'di holds that someone who has faith but whose bad deeds outweigh his good does not remain in the Fire forever. The precise nature of the balance remains a point of interpretation between literal and figurative readings.

This verse describes the fate of those whose scales are light on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that whoever's bad deeds outweigh the good has lost his own soul by squandering it, cut off from God's mercy, and will remain forever in Hell. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi specify that these are the disbelievers, whose deeds carry no weight before God. The commentators agree that the 'lafh' means the burning and scorching of the flame, and that the 'kulūh' is the drawing back of the lips that exposes the teeth, as al-Tabari shows by quoting a line of al-A'sha. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relay the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, in which the upper lip is drawn up to the middle of the head and the lower lip hangs down to the navel. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the clause 'they will abide therein forever' may be an apposition or a second predicate. Ibn 'Atiyya presents the weighing as a way of making the proof manifest in terms people understand. Several commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, report traditions about the trumpet and the confusion of that day that makes family ties count for nothing, while Ibn Sa'di stresses that losing one's own soul is the greatest loss. Al-Razi notes that the verse means the effect of kinship is removed, not kinship itself. Al-Jaza'iri and al-Tafsir al-Muyassar summarise the verse as the condemnation of those whose deeds lack weight, above all through associating others with God.

This verse describes the fate of those whose scales are light: the Fire scorches their faces, and they are grimacing within it, lips drawn back and teeth bared. The commentators agree that lafh means the burning touch of the fire, and that kulûh is the drawing back of the lips so the teeth show. Ibn Abbas explains it as scowling, and al-Tabari supports this meaning with a line of verse by al-A'sha. A hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, reported by al-Tirmidhi and cited by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, describes this disfigurement in detail. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi report that lafh and nafh share the same meaning, with lafh being more intense, as al-Zajjaj says. Some readers recited kalihun without the alif, a reading noted by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. The verse connects to what follows, where they are reproached: were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the face is singled out because it is the noblest part of a person, and that showing its state more strongly deters from the sins that lead to the Fire.

God tells the people of the Fire, in a tone of rebuke, that His verses were recited to them in the world and they denied them. The commentators understand these verses to be the Qur'an, which warns and admonishes. Faced with this reproach, the damned admit that their wretchedness overcame them and kept them from guidance, and that they were a people who had gone astray. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and those who follow them explain that the word shiqwatuna (our wretchedness) means what was decreed for them and known beforehand to God, whereas az-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the bad outcome that resulted from their own deeds, so that the verse is a confession of guilt. Al-Mawardi offers that this wretchedness may be desire, or a good opinion of oneself combined with a bad opinion of others. The readers Hamza and al-Kisa'i read shaqawatuna with an alif, while the others read shiqwatuna; the scholars treat these as two forms with the same meaning. Most commentators agree that the purpose is to establish the proof against them, since the messengers came and the verses were recited to them, and they agree on the conclusion of the passage: the divine answer, 'Be silent in it and do not speak to Me,' ends all hope.

This verse describes what the people of the Fire say when they are rebuked by being reminded of the Quranic verses they denied. They admit their error and say that their wretchedness (shiqwa) overcame them. The commentators agree that shiqwa refers to the condition that led to a bad end. Al-Tabari and Mujahid take it to mean what was decreed for them in God's knowledge and in the Mother of the Book, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that they were too wretched to submit to the proof and so went astray. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as a passion that dominated them and produced a bad end through their evil deeds. Al-Jubba'i, cited by al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, identifies shiqwa with forbidden pleasures, the cause being named for its effect. Al-Qurtubi judges that the best reading is that their desires and pleasures overpowered them, since these lead to misery. Al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi reject the idea of a predetermined decree offered as an excuse, since God records only what a person will freely choose, and they see the words as an admission of guilt.

On the recitation, the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read shiqwatuna with a kasra and no alif, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read shaqawatuna with a fatha and an alif. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi state that both readings are well known and have the same meaning. Their confession that they were a people who had gone astray is taken by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to mean straying from guidance and truth, and al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi note that it is an acknowledgment rather than an excuse.

Their following plea to be returned to the world is refused by the words 'Be silent in it and do not speak to Me', which Ibn Kathir reads as meaning that no way out remains.

This verse records the plea of the people of the Fire on the Day of Judgment: they ask their Lord to bring them out, and promise that if they return to their former disbelief and sins, they will be wrongdoers against themselves. Most commentators understand the request as a wish to return to the worldly life, while some see it as a plea for relief or respite rather than a real hope of escape. God's answer is final: "Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that this is their last utterance, after which they produce only groans and wails and lose all hope. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi relay long narratives about the guardian Malik and repeated pleas over vast periods, which Ibn 'Atiyya judged unreliable though sound in meaning. On the word shiqwa, al-Zamakhshari takes it as the evil end God knew they deserved through their deeds, while al-Jubba'i, al-Razi and al-Baydawi read it as their pursuit of forbidden pleasures that led them there. Abu al-Su'ud rejects a fatalist reading, since God records only what He knows people will freely choose. The variant readings shiqwatuna and shaqawatuna are treated as two forms of the same word.

This verse records God's reply to the people of the Fire who ask to be brought out and returned to the world. He tells them to be silent in the Fire in humiliation, and the word ikhsa'u, as the commentators explain, is the command used to drive away a dog, meaning to be repelled and disgraced. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as rejection and removal, while Ibn 'Atiyya notes its use in chasing dogs. As for the phrase 'and do not speak to Me', the commentators differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as a prohibition on speaking about lifting the punishment or returning to life, whereas al-Hasan, cited by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, holds that it is the last word the damned will utter, after which there remains only sighing and wailing. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that what follows is a barking like that of dogs. Al-Razi observes that this is not a legal command, since there is no obligation in the Hereafter, but a prohibition on speaking about the lifting of the punishment. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a rebuke meant to cut off all hope of deliverance, and al-Alusi describes it as the utmost despair. The narrations about the repeated pleas of the damned, including those reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Amr, vary; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the long report attributed to this context unreliable, though its meaning is sound. Al-Sa'di and al-Alusi add that this reply is harder for the guilty to bear than the Fire itself.

This verse records that God answers the damned, who asked to be brought out of the Fire, with rejection and humiliation, and then gives the reason: there was a group of His servants who used to say in the world, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us, for You are the best of the merciful'. The unbelievers mocked them so much that this made them forget the remembrance of God. The commentators agree that the group refers to the believers. They differ on who exactly they were. Mujahid, Muqatil and Ibn Kathir name Bilal, 'Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Salman and the poor among the Companions, whom the leaders of Quraysh ridiculed, while al-Baydawi and al-Samʻani mention the Companions in general or the People of the Bench. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the verse applies to any humble believer mocked in any age. On the reading of 'sikhriyyan' with kasra or damma there is disagreement: al-Khalil and Sibawayh regard them as two dialect forms with the same meaning, whereas al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' say the kasra means mockery and the damma means subjugation. Al-Zamakhshari notes that attributing the forgetting to the believers is a figure of speech, since they were its cause. Most draw from the verse a warning against scorning the weak and an encouragement to patience and sincere supplication.

This verse recalls that a group of God's believing servants used to say, in this life, 'Our Lord, we believe; forgive us and have mercy on us,' while the disbelievers mocked them so much that the mockery kept them from remembering God, and they laughed at them. The commentators differ on who these believers were: al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya link them to the weak Muslims of Quraysh, and Muqatil and Mujahid name Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb and Khabbab, while others take the phrase to mean the Companions in general or the People of the Suffa. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi consider the verse to apply broadly to anyone in a similar situation. On the reading of sukhriyyan, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi report that Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a damma, and the rest with a kasra. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh hold that the two forms are synonymous, while al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' distinguish the kasra as mockery in speech from the damma as subjection through action. The phrase 'made you forget My remembrance' is attributed to the believers because they were the cause of that forgetting, as al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain. Al-Qurtubi draws from the verse a warning against mocking the weak and the poor, and Ibn Kathir uses it to describe the disbelievers' derision of the believers.

This verse states that God has today rewarded the believers whom the disbelievers mocked in this world, because of their patience under insult and persecution and their obedience to God. They are the ones who triumph, saved from the Fire and granted Paradise. It comes within a dialogue with the damned, who are told to remain in the Fire and not to speak, and this mention of the believers serves to grieve them by showing them the fate of those they despised. The commentators agree that these believers were poor companions of the Prophet such as Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab and Suhayb, and that the mockers were the leaders of Quraysh, though some extended the meaning to any weak person ridiculed. On the reading of sikhriyyan, al-Khalil and Sibawayh held that the kasra and damma forms are two dialects with the same meaning. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' distinguished them, taking the kasra as mockery by speech and the damma as subjugation by action. Ibn Atiyya judged the kasra more fitting to the context, while al-Tabari considered both readings equally valid. On anna-hum with a fatha, the success is read as the object of the reward, while inna-hum with a kasra makes it an independent statement that they, not you, are the winners. Several commentators note that the patience meant includes patience both under affliction and in obedience.

God asks the people of the Fire how many years they stayed on earth, and they answer that they stayed only a day or part of a day, for the intensity of their torment made them forget how long they had lived, so they refer the question to those who can count. Most commentators take 'the earth' to mean the life of this world, while others understand the graves, and the question is a rebuke to those who denied the resurrection. al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir agree that the answer belittles the duration compared with the eternity of punishment, and that worldly life, however long, is brief. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi attribute the forgetting to the severity of the torment; al-Qurtubi reports from Ibn 'Abbas that the punishment is lifted between the two blasts of the trumpet, so they forgot what they had endured. As for 'the counters', Mujahid identifies them as the angels who record human deeds, Qatada as the reckoners, and al-Tabari holds that the phrase admits both meanings without a decisive proof for either; Ibn 'Atiyya notes that its apparent sense is anyone possessing that capacity. On the reading, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read 'Qul' in the imperative, while the others read 'Qala' in the past tense; al-Tabari prefers the latter as the more eloquent Arabic usage. Finally, al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur report an opinion that the question concerns the stay in the graves, its aim being to correct their denial of resurrection.

This passage from Surah al-Mu'minun recounts a question God puts to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection about how long they remained on earth. They answer that they stayed a day or part of a day, and they refer the questioner to those who can count. The commentators agree that this answer reflects an underestimation caused by forgetfulness and the intensity of the torment, and that the purpose is to rebuke them and to show how brief their worldly life was compared with what awaits them. Ibn 'Abbas says the torment made them forget how long they had stayed, and al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi report that the punishment is lifted between the two blasts of the trumpet. As for the "counters" (al-'adddin), Mujahid takes them to be the angels who record human deeds, while Qatada takes them to be reckoners. Al-Tabari considers that they may be angels or other beings, and that no proof singles out either. Al-Zamakhshari understands that they cannot count and so must ask someone able to do so. On the meaning of "in the earth", al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and most commentators take it to mean the graves, that is, the state of death, whereas others take it to mean earthly life. On the reading, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb as an imperative, "Say", while the rest read it as a past tense; al-Tabari prefers the past tense. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the words "You stayed only a little" confirm their claim when measured against their eternity in the Fire.

This passage from Surah al-Mu'minun recounts a question put to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: how many years did you remain on earth? They answer that they stayed only a day or part of a day, so overwhelmed are they by punishment, and they refer the question to those who can count, such as the angels or the reckoners. God replies that their stay was brief, and that had they known it they would have acted accordingly. The commentators understand this stay in two ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take it to be their life in this world, while Ibn 'Atiyya and most early interpreters take it to be their time in the grave, since they had denied resurrection. Al-Razi allows both readings and leans toward seeing the question as a rebuke meant to make them regret the beliefs they held in the world. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain their low estimate by the suffering that makes time seem short, or by the fact that what has passed seems as if it never was. Ibn 'Abbas reports that God made them forget the torment between the two blasts of the trumpet. The readers differ between qala (he said) and qul (say), a reading associated with Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir in some places, and the scholars note it matches the codices of certain regions. As for the next verse, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God did not create human beings in vain, without reckoning, while al-Razi sees in it proof that resurrection is necessary to separate the righteous from the wrongdoers.

This verse rebukes those who deny the Resurrection by asking whether they think God created them in vain, without purpose or wisdom, and that they will never be brought back to Him for judgment. The commentators agree that the verse is a reproach and a refutation of this denial. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain 'abathan' as futility or play, with no aim. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain that it means creation without wisdom, and that the word is either a circumstantial or an object of purpose; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi accept both readings. Al-Tabari holds that the two readings of the verb for 'being returned' are close in meaning, since being brought back to God after death is a form of returning. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim, draw from this that humans were created to worship God, to obey His commands and prohibitions, and to be recompensed. Al-Razi links the verse to the necessity of the Resurrection, without which the obedient could not be distinguished from the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir also reports narrations about reciting this verse as a remedy, which most commentators do not treat as a legal basis.

In this verse God exalts Himself above what the polytheists attribute to Him, whether partners or offspring. He is the true King, to whom sovereignty rightly belongs, there is no god but Him, and He is the Lord of the noble Throne. The commentators agree that the verse answers the idea that God created people in vain, without wisdom, resurrection or reckoning, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir say the Throne is called noble because mercy, good and blessing descend from it, or because it is attributed to the Most Noble. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi prefer to read "the true King" as the one to whom kingship rightly belongs, since everything comes from Him and returns to Him, or as the one whose rule never ends. Regarding the phrase "he has no proof for it," al-Tabari and Mujahid understand it as having no argument or evidence. Al-Zamakhshari treats it as a necessary qualifier added for emphasis, while al-Baydawi sees it as a warning that holding a belief without evidence is forbidden. The commentators explain that the reckoning of one who calls upon another god besides God belongs to his Lord, and that disbelievers will not prosper. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy note that the reading of "innahu" with a fatha, attributed to al-Hasan and Qatada, gives a causal sense. Readings also differ on the vowelling of "karim" and "innahu", as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi point out. The passage ends with the command to the Prophet to ask for forgiveness and mercy, so the surah closes by contrasting the success of believers with the failure of disbelievers.

This verse states that whoever calls on another god alongside God without any proof will have his reckoning with his Lord, and that the disbelievers will not prosper. Commentators largely agree on the overall meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that "without proof" means without argument or evidence, and that there is no justification for associating partners with God. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take the phrase as a necessary qualification rather than a restriction, emphasising that shirk cannot be supported. Al-Razi draws from it that any belief lacking demonstration must be rejected, which supports reflection over blind imitation. On the word "reckoning", al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as the repayment for the evil deed, while al-Mawardi offers two readings: the accounting on the Day of Resurrection or recompense. Ibn 'Ashur, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shinqiti regard the restriction "with his Lord" as genuine, so that the reckoning belongs to God alone. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, note the reading of al-Hasan and Qatada, "annahu", which gives the sense that his reckoning is the absence of success. Ibn 'Ashur and Sayyid Qutb highlight that the surah opens with the success of the believers and closes with the failure of the disbelievers. The reports cited about this surah are judged weak or mursal by Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari. The verse ends with the command to the Prophet to ask forgiveness and mercy.

In the closing verse of the surah, God commands His Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to say: My Lord, forgive me and have mercy on me, and You are the best of those who show mercy. Al-Tabari explains that this means cover my sins with Your pardon, have mercy on me by accepting my repentance and sparing me punishment, and that You are the best of those who show mercy to one who has sinned by accepting his repentance. Commentators generally agree that forgiveness means erasing a sin and concealing it from people, while mercy means guiding and supporting a person in word and deed. Most of them, including al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, present the supplication as a teaching for the believers to follow their Prophet, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari see it as embracing both the Prophet and his community. Al-Nasafi notes that when God's mercy reaches someone it spares him the need for anyone else's mercy, while others' mercy does not spare him from God's. Abu al-Su'ud observes that the Prophet, who has already been forgiven, is commanded to ask for forgiveness, which shows how important this request is. Al-Biqa'i connects the verse with the opening of the surah, which begins with the success of the believers and ends with a plea for divine mercy. Al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di read it as a reminder not to rely on one's deeds but to cling to the mercy of the Lord.
